articles.title: The Tejano singer trying to win back Latinos who voted for Trump, one quinceañera at a time
articles.summary: Bobby Pulido has a strategy: show up at the 15th birthday parties that are a rite of passage in the Texas borderlands – and flip a key House district for Dem...
articles.body:
It took all of two minutes for Bobby Pulido's electoral stealth weapon to come into play. The Tejano music star turned Democratic congressional candidate had barely begun canvassing in the high school football stadium in Edinburg, Texas, when a 15-year-old girl came rushing up to him.

"Señor Pulido! Señor Pulido!" she cried. A few months ago, she told him, he had made a surprise appearance at her quinceañera, the coming-of-age girls' 15th birthday party that is a rite of passage in these US borderlands.

He had serenaded her with Desvelado , his blockbuster love song, which though released three decades ago retains a treasured place in Tejano – that is Hispanic Texan – culture.

The brief encounter gave a glimpse into one of the key dynamics of Pulido's bid to flip Texas's 15th congressional district. He calls it the "quinceañera strategy".

The tactic was handed to him, inadvertently, by his rival, the two-term incumbent Republican congresswoman Monica De La Cruz. In March, she posted a video deriding her opponent as a lowly quinceañera singer.

The election, she said, "isn't about who you want performing at your niece's quinceañera. It's about who you trust with your family's future."

Pulido pounced. He counter-posted his own video in which he accused De La Cruz of belittling a cherished local tradition and encouraged families in the district planning a quinceañera to invite him. "I'd be honored to stop by and celebrate with you," he said.

Within 24 hours, Pulido's campaign had been inundated with over 1,000 invitations. By the time the Guardian went canvassing with him in September, that number had surpassed 5,000.

He has now performed at 81 quinceañeras and counting. Each one is attended by scores of family and friends, most of whom are eligible voters and many of whom livestream the event on their smartphones, broadcasting it to additional scores of eligible voters.

"She presented us with an opportunity for a very unique kind of field plan," Abel Prado, Pulido's campaign manager, said.

Pulido, 53, is hoping to convert the quinceañera strategy and the rest of the tireless retail politics that he is doing into a winning political formula. His mission: to take back the congressional seat, and in the process both help the national Democratic party regain control of the US House and teach it a lesson or two about Mexican American politics.

It's not just that flipping Texas 15 could give Democrats the edge they need to take back control of the House of Representatives. The stakes are also huge for the Rio Grande valley itself, the overwhelmingly Hispanic border region in south Texas that for over a century was solidly Democratic but swung hard for Donald Trump in 2024.

Trump won the district, which is 81% Mexican American and which runs for over 300 miles from the border to San Antonio, by 18 points.

How Pulido fares in the November midterm elections could have ripple effects for fellow Democrat James Talarico's currently neck-and-neck fight for a US Senate seat against the state's scandal-ridden Republican attorney general, Ken Paxton. Talarico's chance of success is also heavily dependent on Latino turnout.

And in the widest sense, Pulido's message has bearings on the national Democratic party as it debates how to counter the dramatic inroads made by Trump two years ago when he smashed records and garnered 55% of Texas's Hispanic vote.

Pulido made sure to display his Tejano stripes as he strutted around the Edinburg stadium, while cheerleaders and a marching band filled the night air with colour and noise. Dressed in jeans and denim shirt, cowboy boots and hat, he moved confidently through the crowd of high-school football fans.

He shook the hand of everyone he met, chatting to supporters on both sides of the bleachers – a calculated move as both high school teams, Sabrecats and Yellowjackets, are in the 15th district. (The Sabrecats won 31-14.)

And yet almost everyone in attendance was too young to vote – so what was the point?

"To win re-election," Pulido quipped, without missing a beat. Then, with more reflection, he added: "If you treat kids good, their parents will like you."

Pulido has a catchphrase : "Any occasion, big or small." He means it. The football game was the 526th campaign event he had attended in person. His record is 12 such stops in a single day.

When Pulido sat down to talk with the Guardian, he emphasised accessibility was a critical element of his campaign. It's his answer, he said, to the increasingly polarised left-right media bubbles that keep voters divided.

"The only way I can break through is to actually get in front of people the old-fashioned way. Then people can hear me. They can look me in the eye, and decide for themselves whether I'm full of shit or not."

Direct connection with voters also allows Pulido, who has roots stretching back seven generations in the Rio Grande valley, to play his ace card: his near-universal name recognition in the region.

Desvelado ("sleepless") was his first, and is still his biggest, hit – the 1995 album of the same name went platinum, and the song has been played 615m times on Spotify. He has won two Latin Grammys for best Tejano album; the day before we met he celebrated yet another nomination for the award, for Una Tuya, Una Mía, Vol 2.

If the massive popularity of Desvelado gives him an entree with younger and middle-aged Tejanos, he can count on his father to grab the attention of older voters. José Roberto Pulido, 75, is a Tejano music star in his own right, having enjoyed a large local following in the 1970s and 80s.

In Pulido's analysis, Trump lured so many of these Tejano voters away from the Democratic party in 2024 because he spoke to their longing for the American dream. There's a popular phrase in the valley: "We know we're broke, but don't tell us we're poor."

Pulido said: "If you're poor, you've already lost; if you're broke, you could still make it one day. Trump kind of won because of that message. 'Look at me, I'm rich, and some of my richness will transfer to you' – that was music to people's ears."

Trump's promise to close the US-Mexico border also spoke to many people in the valley. The disruption caused by record numbers of undocumented immigrants crossing into the US during the Biden administration was especially felt in this frontier zone, and many Tejano US citizens bridled against it despite their own immigrant heritage.

"Under Biden, the border was chaotic," Pulido said. "The tent cities, the visible hardship, so many coming across."

Since the return of Trump to the White House, however, Pulido believes that the president has squandered much of that goodwill. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made Texas the ground zero of its mass deportation efforts, notably so given the central position the state commands within Trump's Maga universe.

Figures compiled by the Deportation Data Project show that ICE made 12,086 arrests in July in Texas. That was almost twice the number in the next most intensely targeted states, Florida (7,405) and California (6,464).

Pulido is convinced that Trump will pay a price in November for this blanket assault on Texas immigrants. "People are angry, ICE enforcement is splitting up families and spreading fear. And it's hurting our economy. There's not a building in the Rio Grande valley that was put up without immigrant hands. None."

He added: "There is a reckoning coming, that's for sure. I see it. We've polled it. People don't like what the Republican party is doing."

The most recent survey of the 15th district, from Texas Southern University , puts Pulido five points ahead of De La Cruz (50% to 45%). Among Latino likely voters, the gap widens to 25 points (60% to 35%).

"This election is showing that the Trump bubble is burst," the co-author of the opinion poll, Mark Jones, professor of political science at Rice University, said. "We did see a temporary shift towards Trump among Latino voters, but now we're coming back to a more standard status quo."

The Guardian spoke to several 15th district voters who two years ago enthusiastically cast their ballots for Trump yet who have grown disaffected and disillusioned.

Yajaira Martinez, 43, is a naturalized citizen who came to the US from Mexico when she was six. In 2024, she voted for Trump because she believed his promises about bringing down prices and improving the economy, and because she supported his desire for a stronger border.

She heard him pledge to remove undocumented immigrants with criminal records. "If you want to take the criminals out of the country, by all means go ahead," she said.

But she did not expect the ICE dragnet of hardworking people trying to make a go for their families. She knows several people who have been deported even though they had legitimate work permits.

"ICE is breaking the law, they are assaulting, they are chasing down. They are terrorising. This administration doesn't care about anybody's rights."

Juan Cantu, 66, was born in Mexico but lives in the US, and as a naturalized citizen is entitled to vote. He makes an income both as a cabinet maker and rancher.

He voted for Trump in 2024 because he was fed up with Democrats talking about social issues such as abortion and trans people using women's bathrooms, and he thought Trump would be on his side as un trabajador , a worker.

But he's been appalled as he watches "the politics of Trump spinning out of control, harming so many working people". The Iran war, which he said he does not understand, and tariffs have pushed the diesel that powers his tractor to $6 a gallon, and that's a problem.

As for Pulido, Cantu likes his father's Tejano music. "That's the music of my época ," he said. And he warms to the candidate's politics. "From what I've heard, he wants to help the poor, the working people."

Juan Pablo Lopez, 41, a first-generation Mexican American born in the US, is the owner of a real estate and construction company in McAllen. He voted for Trump because he liked the way he spoke the language of business.

In the past year, though, it's turned sour for Lopez. He estimates that about 60 of his co-workers and friends have disappeared, rounded up by ICE and detained then deported.

He said he had come to conclusion that Trump is not the friend of Tejanos. "Everybody here believed in him, and instead of helping us, he's hurting us."

As for his vote in November, it's complicated. Lopez said he likes Pulido. "I was born and raised with his music. He's a family guy, and I like that he's very conservative."

What he doesn't like is that Pulido is running as a Democrat, a party he thinks has a "Robin Hood mentality". "They take from the rich to give to the poor – let's give everybody food stamps, let's make sure everybody's on housing. I'm a hardworking American."

That leaves him in a bind. "I'm faced with a very hard decision of who I'm going to vote for. I don't want to vote Democrat, but look at what Trump has done to us."

It's Pulido's challenge to overcome the hesitation of voters like Lopez. He must harness their patent anger towards Trump's handling of immigration and the economy, and persuade them that not all Democrats are leftist progressives.

As he faces this challenge, Pulido is careful to emphasise his conservative convictions while avoiding talking in party political terms. The race is not about Democrat versus Republican, but about Bobby versus Monica.

"I do not mention blue waves. Not ever."

There is a populist side to Pulido's politics that bears comparison to Bernie Sanders. He denounces "crony capitalism" and demands that corporate money is removed from US elections.

Pulido doesn't have health insurance because "it's not worth it".

"I should not feel obligated to feed those monsters. Health insurance companies get away with it, and doctors can't even be doctors any more," he said.

Beneath the populist patina, his innate cultural conservatism – typical of this border region – is glaringly apparent. He is a man of faith, and is personally opposed to abortion though his policy is that he would not impose his views on anybody else: "Pro-life is a choice too. It's my choice," he said.

He opposes restrictions on oil and gas extraction, including fracking, as they account for a significant proportion of the valley's jobs. He wants the border to remain locked down even after Trump has gone, though he wants that to be done humanely.

There's no doubting his support for the second amendment. He named his son Remington, after the Remington 700 bolt-action rifle that he loves.

If you described a politician with that set of convictions to a person in Brooklyn or Santa Monica they might assume he were a moderate Republican. So what makes him a Democrat?

"I'm a Democrat because I lead with my democratic heart," he said. "I understand that there are people out there who need help, and that it's my obligation as a Catholic and as a Christian to do what I can to help my fellow neighbor."

In all this, there is an implicit criticism of the national leadership of the Democratic party and what he regards as its coastal elite prejudices.

"In music, you have to know your audience. I'm smart enough to know that you don't take a symphonic orchestra to the dancehall – people want to dance. But that's what my party is doing, taking the east coast and west coast politics of the liberal elites and bringing them to where they do not resonate."

Warming to the theme, he said: "What plays well in New York City likely won't play well among Democratic voters in the valley. The party has become too one-size-fits-all, and that's a big mistake."

His main takeaway from his months running for congressional office is that Democrats "let other people define us".

"When I first told people in this district that I was running as a Democrat, their automatic assumption was that I was going to take away their guns, that I was for trans in women's sports, that I was going to take away their oil and gas jobs," he said. "That's the narrative they were fed by Republicans."

As the 3 November election gets closer, and the temperature of the race rises, De La Cruz has tried to stall Pulido's advance by hitting him with negative attack ads casting him as a "corrupt liberal celebrity". In particular, she has focused on revelations that an accordionist in Pulido's band who played on the recording of Desvelado later became a registered sex offender.

De La Cruz has accused Pulido of "endangering our families". He counters that he only discovered his band member's sex crimes record years later.

The Republican has also charged Pulido with demeaning voters, basing the claim on a 2020 video that has resurfaced in which he is seen laughing as a comedy host made remarks about women's bodies following childbirth and on past social media posts in which he used racist and homophobic slurs . Pulido has admitted that some of his comments crossed the line and apologised for them. But he argues that De La Cruz has supported a president who has repeatedly attacked women's appearances.

So far there is insufficient data from opinion polls to know whether the mud is sticking.

Republican efforts to win congressional seats in south Texas through redistricting may also backfire on De La Cruz. The 15th district was redrawn with the aim of preserving her lead while at the same time attempting to flip neighboring seats from the Democrats.

As a result almost two-thirds of the voters in the reconfigured 15th district are new to De La Cruz, with many voters having little or no idea who she is.

That matters when she is up against someone with almost universal name recognition like Pulido. "When I saw the map, I was very happy," he said with a grin.

Asked to comment on Pulido's political record and the state of the race, De La Cruz's campaign manager, James Shook, described Pulido as "a silver-spooned scumbag who enabled a sex predator".

"Anyone starstruck by this pedo-protecting loser should be ashamed of themselves," he said in the statement.

There is a bittersweetness to the looming election for Pulido. He is potentially poised to pull off a historic victory that would send him to Washington where a whole new political life would await him.

But it would mark the end of his other life as a Tejano musician. Last year he embarked on a farewell tour, and just before we met his final performance was announced.

It will take place in Edinburg, 17 days before the election. He's calling it La Última Desvelada.

articles.title: Fim da 6x1: Senado inicia debate com ausência dos senadores do PL | G1
articles.standfirst: Apoiadores do presidente Lula discursaram em favor de reduzir a jornada de trabalho no país; Alcolumbre sinaliza votação na próxima semana.
articles.summary: Senadores iniciam debate sobre o fim da escala 6x1 com foco na redução da jornada de trabalho e previsão de votação da PEC para a próxima semana.
articles.body:
O plenário do Senado Federal realizou nesta terça-feira (6) a primeira discussão da Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) que acaba com a escala 6x1 sem redução de salário.

A sessão teve presença da maioria de senadores que apoiam o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), discursos foram somente a favor da aprovação da medida.

Por outro lado, a maioria dos senadores do PL nem mesmo foi à reunião do Senado sobre o tema. Senadores aliados do candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) tentam evitar que a PEC seja votada e defendem que outro texto sobre o tema seja analisado (entenda mais abaixo).

Dos 15 senadores que o PL tem atualmente, seis registraram presença: Efraim Filho (PB), Izalci Lucas (DF), Eduardo Gomes (TO), Magno Malta (ES), Wilder Morais (GO) e Marcio Bittar (AC). Flávio não participou da discussão, nem de forma remota, mesmo estando em Brasília. A sessão foi semipresencial.

Antes da discussão, o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), sinalizou que deve colocar a PEC do fim da 6x1 em votação na próxima semana. Durante a sessão, Alcolumbre recebeu e tirou foto com líderes sindicais favoráveis à PEC.

O presidente do Senado afirmou que os senadores devem votar "com a sua consciência e com a sua convicção", se o trabalhador merece ou não mais um dia de descanso.

Alcolumbre disse também querer seguir o rito normal, sem apressar as discussões. Assim, o Senado deve fazer mais quatro sessões de discussão antes de votar a proposta em primeiro turno. Para uma PEC ser aprovada, ela precisa de 49 votos favoráveis em duas votações.

Entre os governistas, o clima ainda é de lutar para aprovar o texto em dois turnos antes do segundo turno. Apostam ainda em expor integrantes da oposição que tentem evitar a votação do fim da 6x1. Integrantes do PL e Republicanos devem se reunir na quarta-feira (7) para definir uma estratégia e evitar a votação.

Nesta terça-feira, Flávio Bolsonaro foi questionado sobre a PEC do governo e, mais uma vez, defendeu a proposta alternativa. O texto da oposição prevê a possibilidade de redução da jornada, com redução proporcional do salário.

Carteira de Trabalho Digital — Foto: Gil Leonardi/ImprensaMG

Entre os senadores que discursaram nesta terça-feira (6), nenhum se disse contra mudar a jornada de trabalho para que os trabalhadores tenham dois dias de descanso remunerado.

O primeiro a discursar foi o senador Paulo Paim (PT-RS) que está no último ano de mandato e no encerramento de sua carreira política. Paim defende o fim da 6x1 há anos, como lembrado por seus pares.

"Olhem para o ser humano, olhem para o trabalhador, olhem para as famílias, olhem para os idosos, olhem para os jovens, olhem para as pessoas com deficiência, olhem para quem acorda de madrugada, olhem para quem pega transporte, olhem para quem trabalha seis dias para descansar um, porque, no fundo, esta não é uma discussão sobre quatro horas ou menos, é uma discussão sobre quatro horas a mais de vida por semana, é uma discussão sobre o direito de ter tempo”, disse Paim.

Já o senador Oriovisto Guimarães (PSDB-PR) disse que não é contra a redução, mas criticou o texto atual da proposta. O senador defendeu que discordâncias não são para adiar a PEC.

“Sou favorável a mudar a escala 6x1 para 5x2. Sou favorável, não me diga que sou contra. Mas é preciso ver os efeitos colaterais. A questão do prazo é fundamental. Não se pode exigir que uma transformação desse tipo seja feita em dois meses. É irracional. Não se pode fazer isso do dia para a noite", disse Oriovisto.

Atualmente, a transição da jornada é de 14 meses, Se aprovada, a PEC deve seguir a seguinte cronologia:

em dois meses, redução da jornada semanal para 42 horas, com dois dias de repouso semanal remunerado;

em um ano após esses dois meses, redução da jornada semanal para 40 horas.

articles.title: Fim da escala 6x1: Lula defende jornada 5x2 e critica Flávio | G1
articles.standfirst: Em uma publicação nas redes sociais, Lula defendeu uma jornada de cinco dias de trabalho e dois dias de descanso por semana, sem redução salarial.
articles.summary: Lula defende o fim da escala 6x1 e a jornada de cinco dias sem corte no salário, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro propõe carga horária flexível.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) voltou a defender nesta terça-feira (6) o fim da escala de trabalho 6x1 e afirmou que quer ver a redução da jornada "sair do papel" e que o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), candidato à Presidência da República, é contra.

"Já Flávio Bolsonaro é contra. Para ele, quem trabalhar menos tem que ganhar menos. Queria ver ele explicar para uma mãe de família qual conta ela deixa de pagar para poder descansar. A comida? A luz? O aluguel? Quem vive de salário sabe que isso não é escolha", disse Lula .

Em uma publicação nas redes sociais, Lula defendeu uma jornada de cinco dias de trabalho e dois dias de descanso por semana, sem redução salarial.

"Na hora que o Senado começa a votar a máscara vai começar a cair. A gente vai ver quem, efetivamente, quer que o povo tenha uma vida mais digna, que descanse mais, que possa cuidar mais da família, ou se vai estabelecer essa jornada em que as pessoas só têm um dia para descansar", afirmou.

O presidente afirmou que a votação da PEC vai proporcionar que a sociedade brasileira conheça "quem é quem" na política e que a votação é o "primeiro teste" para que o PL diga "o que quer desse país".

"O dia de hoje é importante pelo seguinte: porque o meu adversário, ele vai ter que tomar uma decisão. Se ele vai mandar a bancada do partido dele votar favorável ao fim da jornada de trabalho 6x1 ou vai aprovar uma nova escala", disse Lula.

Em declaração na sede da coordenação da campanha, Lula disse que o PL está tentando atrapalhar a votação da PEC que acaba com a jornada sem redução de salário.

A proposta em discussão no Congresso Nacional estabelece jornada máxima de 40 horas semanais, divididas em cinco dias de trabalho e dois de descanso, sem redução salarial. A proposta começou a ser discutida nesta terça pelo plenário do Senado Federal.

"Eu estou confiante que o Alcolumbre vai colocar em votação. Estou confiando que o Senado vai repetir a decisão que já foi tomada pela Câmara e estou confiante que o PL vai demonstrar se tem coragem ou não votar a favor do fim dessa escala", disse Lula.

Entre os governistas, o clima ainda é de lutar para aprovar o texto em dois turnos antes do segundo turno. Apostam ainda em expor integrantes da oposição que tentem evitar a votação do fim da 6x1. Integrantes do PL e Republicanos devem se reunir na quarta-feira (7) para definir uma estratégia e evitar a votação.

O texto já foi aprovado pela Câmara e pela Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) do Senado e ainda precisa passar por dois turnos de votação no plenário do Senado.

"Hoje, o Senado voltou a discutir uma mudança que pode fazer uma diferença enorme na vida de milhões de brasileiros e brasileiras: o fim da escala 6x1. E eu quero ver essa conquista sair do papel", afirmou Lula.

"O que defendemos são 5 dias de trabalho e 2 dias de folga por semana, sem redução de salário. Porque o trabalhador e a trabalhadora querem melhorar de vida, mas também querem tempo para viver, descansar, cuidar da saúde e estar com a família", prosseguiu.

Flávio já se posicionou contra o fim da escala 6x1 nos moldes propostos pelo Congresso. O candidato do PL defende uma jornada flexível, negociada diretamente entre empregado e empregador. Esse modelo poderia incluir redução de salário caso houvesse diminuição da carga horária.

Em agosto, durante encontro com empresários na Federação das Indústrias do Estado de São Paulo (Fiesp), Flávio defendeu que o trabalhador tivesse liberdade para escolher a própria carga horária como alternativa à extinção da escala 6x1.

Questionado sobre o tema nesta terça, Flávio Bolsonaro afirmou que defende dar mais liberdade para que o trabalhador escolha a própria carga horária. Como exemplo, citou mães que não conseguem cumprir uma jornada de oito horas por não terem com quem deixar os filhos.

“Eu tenho uma proposta infinitamente melhor do que essa proposta que está na mesa, que é dar liberdade para que o trabalhador escolha a sua própria carga horária. Tem muitas mães, por exemplo, que não conseguem trabalhar oito horas por dia porque não têm como deixar seus filhos", disse.

O candidato afirmou que, em seu projeto, essas mães poderiam definir a jornada de acordo com suas necessidades e teriam acesso a um voucher para pagar uma creche privada caso não conseguissem vaga na rede pública.

Para participar é necessário documento de identificação, carteira de trabalho e cópias do currículo. — Foto: FUNTRAB

A discussão ocorre em meio ao segundo turno da eleição presidencial. Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro disputam a Presidência no dia 25 de outubro. No primeiro turno, Flávio recebeu 47,03% dos votos válidos, e Lula, 45,16%.

O fim da escala 6x1 já havia provocado divergências entre os dois candidatos antes da votação. Em agosto, a coordenação da campanha de Flávio tentou evitar que a PEC fosse votada durante o período eleitoral. A avaliação do PL era de que uma mudança dessa dimensão deveria ser discutida com mais profundidade e analisada somente depois das eleições.

articles.title: Bancada ruralista anuncia apoio a Flávio Bolsonaro no segundo turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Flávio Bolsonaro recebeu mais de 56 milhões de votos e enfrentará, no segundo turno, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, candidato do PT à reeleição. Romeu Zema (Novo), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) e a federação União-PP, também anunciaram apoio ao candidato à Presidência.
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro recebeu mais de 56 milhões de votos e enfrentará, no segundo turno, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, candidato do PT à reeleição. Romeu Zema (Novo), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) e a federação União-PP, também anunciaram apoio ao candidato à Presidência.
articles.body:
Membros da bancada ruralista do Congresso Nacional se reuniram com o senador e candidato a Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) nesta terça-feira (6) e declararam apoio a ele no segundo turno das eleições presidenciais.

O anúncio foi feito presidente da Frente Parlamentar Agropecuária (FPA), deputado federal Pedro Lupion (Republicanos-PR), ao lado de Flávio e outros parlamentares.

Segundo o candidato, caso seja eleito, futuro ministro da Agricultura e Pecuária (MAPA) será definido por uma indicação da frente parlamentar.

"Viemos aqui declarar oficialmente o apoio à candidatura do presidente Flávio Bolsonaro. Isso se dá por um motivo muito claro e que está demonstrado em todas as questões econômicas do país", disse Lupion.

Flávio Bolsonaro recebeu mais de 56 milhões de votos e enfrentará, no segundo turno, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, candidato do PT à reeleição, que recebeu 53,8 milhões de votos.

O segundo turno das eleições presidenciais está marcado para o dia 25 de outubro.

No dia 1 de outubro, a FPA manifestou apoio a Flávio no primeiro turno da disputa presidencial.

Em nota, a Frente afirmou que, a partir de 2027, acreditam ser possível "alcançar no Congresso soluções que tragam um novo ambiente econômico de estabilidade, previsibilidade e prosperidade".

"O campo seguirá de pé, com responsabilidade, independência e disposição para garantir a segurança alimentar dos brasileiros e construir o futuro do nosso país", diz a nota.

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) com membros da bancada ruralista do Congresso Nacional — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Mais cedo, a federação formada por União Brasil e Progressistas (União Progressista) também anunciou apoio ao senador no segundo turno da disputa à Presidência da República.

Também nesta terça, o ex-candidato à Presidência da República Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) também declarou que vai apoiar o candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no segundo turno.

Flávio foi a Goiás se reunir com Caiado nesta terça. Após o encontro, o ex-candidato falou sobre sua amizade e relação com o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro antes de declarar seu apoio ao senador. O ex-governador destacou que o apoio seria o desejo do ex-presidente.

"Goiás vai dar a maior vitória ao Flávio Bolsonaro nessa eleição. A mobilização vai ser em tempo integral", disse Ronaldo Caiado.

O ex-governador de Goiás foi o quinto colocado na disputa à Presidência, com 2.605.148 votos. O candidato teve 2,18% dos votos válidos.

Flávio também recebeu apoio do ex-candidato do Novo, Romeu Zema . Nesta segunda-feira (5), Zema afirmou que não iria se omitir e declarou voto a Flávio Bolsonaro.

"Eu não vou me omitir nem ficar em cima do muro nesse momento tão importante. Voto contra o PT. Voto no Flávio Bolsonaro. O Brasil não aguenta mais 4 anos de Lula, nem mais 4 ministros nomeados pelo Lula. Estamos juntos no dia 25, conto com você", afirmou.

Zema foi o sexto colocado na disputa à Presidência e recebeu 326.488 votos. O candidato do Novo obteve 0,27% dos votos válidos, de acordo com o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral.

Augusto Cury (Avante) e Renan Santos (Missão) ficaram nas terceira e quarta posições, respectivamente. Os dois já disseram que não vão apoiar nem Flávio nem Lula.

articles.title: Rogério Marinho é levado a hospital em Brasília após mal-estar | G1
articles.standfirst: Político voltava de evento de campanha em Goiânia e se sentiu mal no voo. Boletim médico cita 'febre associada' e diz que Marinho ficará internado para exames e tratamento clínico.
articles.summary: Coordenador da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro, o senador Rogério Marinho realiza exames em Brasília após apresentar mal-estar em voo vindo de Goiânia.
articles.body:
Rogerio Marinho (PL-RN) — Foto: Jefferson Rudy/Agência Senado

O senador Rogério Marinho ( PL -RN) foi levado a um hospital particular em Brasília , na tarde desta terça-feira (6), para fazer exames após um "mal-estar".

Marinho é um dos coordenadores da campanha do candidato à presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

Em um boletim médico divulgado às 21h15, o DF Star informou que Rogério Marinho teve um "quadro de febre associado a mal-estar".

"No momento, encontra-se internado para realização de exames e tratamento clínico", informou o hospital no documento assinado por três médicos.

Os sintomas foram percebidos quando o político voava de volta a Brasília, após um ato em Goiânia com Flávio, o ex-governador Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) – derrotado no primeiro turno da eleição presidencial – e o governador reeleito, Daniel Vilela ( MDB ).

Em nota divulgada antes do boletim médico, o gabinete afirmou que Marinho foi levado ao hospital "por precaução" e que "passa bem".

articles.title: Gilmar Mendes arquiva investigação de estupro contra vice de Flávio Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: A Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) já havia manifestado pelo indeferimento do pedido de abertura de inquérito.
articles.summary: A Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) já havia manifestado pelo indeferimento do pedido de abertura de inquérito.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro e Alfredo Gaspar em Natal — Foto: Kléber Teixeira/Inter TV Cabugi

O ministro Gilmar Mendes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), determinou o arquivamento de apuração de suposto estupro de vulnerável contra o deputado federal Alfredo Gaspar (PL-AL), candidato a vice-presidente na chapa de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

A Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) já havia manifestado pelo indeferimento do pedido de abertura de inquérito.

De acordo com a PGR, os elementos colhidos nas diligências "não permitiram confirmar a origem das comunicações nem identificar as pessoas diretamente envolvidas nos fatos narrados, tampouco forneceram elementos independentes de corroboração das informações apresentadas pelos noticiantes".

"Não se verifica, no estado atual dos autos, base indiciária suficiente para a instauração do inquérito pretendido. As capturas de tela, os arquivos de áudio, os dados relativos ao endereço eletrônico e à linha telefônica, bem como os relatos colhidos no curso das diligências preliminares, não se mostram suficientemente corroborados entre si nem encontram respaldo em elementos externos e independentes capazes de conferir consistência objetiva às imputações formuladas", diz o ministro Gilmar Mendes na decisão.

A Polícia Federal (PF) havia recebido um pedido de abertura de inquérito para investigar Alfredo Gaspar por suspeita de estupro de vulnerável da senadora Soraya Thronicke (PSB-MS) e do deputado federal Lindbergh Farias (PT-RJ).

Alfredo Gaspar chegou a acionar a Justiça contra os dois parlamentares, alegando que os dois divulgaram informações falsas sobre ele, após os dois comentarem a acusação de estupro.

O caso aconteceu durante uma sessão da Comissão Parlamentar Mista de Inquérito (CPMI) do INSS, do qual Gaspar era relator. Na ocasião Lindbergh chamou Gaspar de "estuprador". Gaspar respondeu chamando o petista de bandido.

articles.title: Cabo Bebeto: quem é o deputado estadual mais votado de Alagoas | G1
articles.standfirst: O parlaentar é policial militar de carreira, está no terceiro mandato e recebeu 99.165 votos nas eleições deste ano.
articles.summary: Conheça a trajetória de Cabo Bebeto, policial militar reeleito para o terceiro mandato como o deputado estadual mais votado de Alagoas nas eleições 2026.
articles.body:
Cabo Bebeto (PL) — Foto: Foto/Assessoria

Luiz Alberto Alves Teixeira, conhecido como Cabo Bebetovoto, foi o deputado estadual mais votado de Alagoas nas Eleições 2026. Candidato pelo PL, ele recebeu 99.165 votos, o equivalente a 5,50% dos votos válidos para a Assembleia Legislativa de Alagoas (ALE). O resultado garantiu a reeleição para o terceiro mandato consecutivo.

A votação de Bebeto ficou 29.795 votos acima da obtida pelo segundo colocado, o deputado Marcelo Victor (MDB), que recebeu 69.370 votos. Ao todo, 27 deputados estaduais foram eleitos em Alagoas para a próxima legislatura.

Cabo Bebeto é um dos mais ferrenhos apoiadores do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro e, em 2026, fez campanha e pediu voto para Flávio Bolsonaro, candidato à presidência, no primeiro turno das eleições deste ano.

Natural de Maceió, Bebeto nasceu em 27 de junho de 1978. É filho de Luiz Wilson e Maria Tereza, é casado e tem três filhos. Antes de entrar para a política, trabalhou com os pais no comércio no Centro da capital alagoana.

À reportagem, o deputado afirmou que não esperava uma votação de quase 100 mil votos e que isso aumenta ainda mais a responsabilidade dele como parlamentar.

"Saber que existem muitas pessoas que pensam de forma parecida comigo me dá ainda mais energia para continuar enfrentando as dificuldades de Alagoas e batendo de frente com o sistema, para que o nosso Estado seja cada vez melhor para os alagoanos".

A trajetória profissional de Bebeto começou longe da Assembleia Legislativa. Em 2002, ele ingressou na Polícia Militar de Alagoas após ser aprovado em concurso público. Começou a carreira como soldado e foi promovido a cabo em 2012.

Durante os 16 anos em que permaneceu na corporação, passou a usar o nome de guerra Cabo Bebeto, que posteriormente adotou como nome político.

A aproximação com a política ocorreu a partir da atuação ligada à categoria dos policiais militares. Em 2017, ele se tornou conselheiro federal da Ordem dos Policiais do Brasil (OPB).

No ano seguinte, disputou pela primeira vez uma eleição para deputado estadual. Filiado ao PSL, foi eleito em 2018 com 31.573 votos. Naquele pleito, também obteve a maior votação entre os candidatos a deputado estadual em Maceió, com 22.066 votos, segundo os dados divulgados à época.

A eleição marcou a entrada de Bebeto na ALE. Ele tomou posse em fevereiro de 2019 e, desde então, permaneceu no Legislativo estadual.

Em 2022, já filiado ao PL, Bebeto disputou novamente uma vaga na ALE e aumentou sua votação. Recebeu 51.721 votos e foi reeleito. Naquele ano, ficou em segundo lugar entre os candidatos a deputado estadual, atrás de Alexandre Ayres, que teve 61.142 votos.

Em Maceió, Bebeto voltou a registrar a maior votação para deputado estadual, com 31.527 votos, de acordo com os dados apresentados em seu perfil eleitoral.

Quatro anos depois da primeira eleição, portanto, a votação de Bebeto havia crescido em mais de 20 mil votos. Em 2026, o crescimento foi ainda maior: os 99.165 votos recebidos representam 47.444 votos a mais que em 2022 e mais de três vezes a votação obtida na primeira eleição, em 2018.

A atuação parlamentar de Cabo Bebeto tem como um dos principais eixos a segurança pública, área diretamente relacionada à sua trajetória anterior na Polícia Militar.

Ele presidiu a Comissão de Direitos Humanos e Segurança Pública da Assembleia Legislativa em diferentes legislaturas. Atualmente, a comissão é oficialmente denominada 9ª Comissão de Direitos Humanos e Segurança Pública, e Bebeto aparece entre os parlamentares que a compõem no período de 2025 a 2027.

Ao longo dos mandatos, também apresentou e relatou projetos relacionados à segurança pública e aos direitos dos agentes da área. O sistema legislativo da Assembleia registra, por exemplo, projetos de sua autoria sobre a situação de profissionais de segurança e sobre regras relacionadas aos militares estaduais.

Entre as propostas apresentadas por Bebeto está um projeto que previa a criação de um memorial em homenagem a profissionais de segurança pública mortos em razão do serviço. A proposta foi aprovada na Assembleia, mas acabou tendo o veto total mantido pelos parlamentares em 2024.

Em 2026, outro projeto de autoria do deputado propôs restringir, nas escolas da rede estadual, a execução de músicas e videoclipes com conteúdos que, segundo a proposta, façam apologia ao crime ou ao uso de drogas ou tenham conteúdo sexual e erótico. A matéria recebeu parecer favorável na comissão de Direitos Humanos e Segurança Pública.

A trajetória política de Bebeto também inclui episódios de disputa eleitoral e atuação nas redes sociais. Em 2022, o Tribunal Regional Eleitoral de Alagoas analisou uma representação que questionava conteúdos publicados pelo então candidato nas redes.

A representação tinha alegação de propaganda eleitoral antecipada negativa e divulgação de fato considerado inverídico. Na ocasião, o TRE-AL negou o pedido de liminar e manteve os conteúdos questionados.

articles.title: Trump administration unveils plan to tie high birth and marriage rates to transit funding
articles.summary: The federal government is seeking to revamp a national program that supports rail and bus rapid transit.
articles.body:
Communities with high birth and marriage rates could soon gain an advantage in securing federal transit money — a long-sought goal of the Trump administration but one that a top Democratic appropriator calls "bizarre and dystopian."

The Federal Transit Administration wants to revamp a multibillion-dollar program that helps state and local authorities fund infrastructure projects such as rail improvements and new bus lanes. Public feedback on the administration's plan, which was rolled out Oct. 1, is being accepted through mid-November.

The idea would fulfill a priority of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to steer grant money to parts of the country with birth and marriage rates higher than the national average, a policy initiative he unveiled shortly after being sworn into office early last year .

Under the transit proposal , the FTA would cover up to 10 percentage points more of a project's costs if an area's average birth and marriage rates meet, exceed or are just below nationwide thresholds.

"Moving forward, the federal government is focusing on smart, affordable projects with high ridership. If you want federal funding, your project needs to align with where communities and families are actually growing," the Transportation Department said in a statement.

But the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee had harsh words for the proposal.

"Tying funding for transit projects to marriage rates and how many babies a woman has is the sort of bizarre and dystopian idea you'd expect in a TV show, not actual policy put forth by the U.S. government — yet here we are," Sen. Patty Murray of Washington state said in a statement.

She said President Donald Trump "wants to weaponize federal grants to wage his backward culture wars and punish Democrats."

Spokespeople for Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), ranking member of the House Appropriations Committee, didn't respond to a request for comment.

A former FTA administrator during the Obama administration also was critical.

"It's throwing a bone to these ideologues who want to incentivize child rearing and marriage," said Peter Rogoff, who previously led Sound Transit in the Seattle area and is now a transportation consultant. "But it's ludicrous on its face to try to achieve that goal through an infrastructure program.

"Does anyone really believe that there are couples out there saying, 'Hey, sweetheart, you and I should get married and raise a passel of kids because a dozen years from now, maybe they'll build light rail out to our neighborhood?'" he asked.

Duffy, who has nine children, has urged young people to tie the knot and " have lots of kids ." He's one of several Cabinet members with big families, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, DHS head Markwayne Mullin and Health and Human Services chief Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The national fertility rate sank to a record low in 2025 — 53.1 births per 1,000 women ages 15 to 44. Trump has said he will be known as the "fertilization president."

The FTA grant program hinges on a lengthy approval process that can take years for applicants to navigate, with money becoming available after a binding grant agreement is executed.

Before reaching the final step, the FTA determines how much of a project's total cost it will cover. The share of federal funding is capped at 60 percent for new, large transit infrastructure and 80 percent for boosting the capacity of existing systems.

For those two types of projects, the administration now wants to calculate the amount it will fund using a formula that, in part, would be based on a transit corridor's average birth and marriage rates. When those rates are at or above national benchmarks, or just below them, the federal share would be increased — rising by up to 10 percentage points.

Under Duffy, DOT has launched a "Make Travel Family Friendly Again" campaign, encouraging airports to create play areas and add nursing rooms at terminals. He also has sought to inspire families to travel around the country via his "The Great American Road Trip" video series .

The birth and marriage rates proposal has yet to be finalized, and it's unknown when it will be. It also wasn't immediately clear which exact communities would benefit from the idea.

The plan is part of a wider effort by the FTA to rewrite its guidance for federal Capital Investment Grants, or CIG. The public can weigh in through Nov. 16.

CIG and a related pilot initiative got $1.7 billion from Congress for fiscal 2026 on top of $1.6 billion in additional funding from the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law.

Projects that previously won money from the program include the ongoing construction of the Gateway rail tunnel between New York and New Jersey and a pending extension of Chicago's Red Line train .

Paul Skoutelas, CEO and president of the American Public Transportation Association, said in a statement the organization is reviewing the FTA plan.

Rogoff, the former FTA administrator, said the framework would "clearly disadvantage" projects in areas with lower birth and marriage rates, adding that federal law doesn't require that this data be relied on when carrying out CIG.

"Obviously, the program is about moving people — not about moving married people or moving parents," he said.

articles.title: The biggest signs that Trump and the GOP are panicking about the midterms
articles.summary: Republicans have had reason to worry about the 2026 midterm elections for quite a while now.
articles.body:
Republicans have had reason to worry about the 2026 midterm elections for a while now.

But there are growing signs that their fears are spilling over into panic — and that the GOP, including President Donald Trump, senses things could get really bad.

That doesn't mean things will turn out that way. And there are plenty of examples of parties overzealously slamming the panic button late in the campaign.

But the Trump-era GOP has generally been a rather sanguine political party, and what we've seen in recent days and weeks is anything but.

Trump has insisted Republicans will do well and that the many polls suggesting otherwise are wrong. But his actions increasingly point in a different direction:

On Monday, he pulled a rare 180 on his highly controversial government-funded political ads, saying they would now be paid for with super PAC funds.

Over the weekend, he started encouraging Republicans to vote by mail , after previously claiming that method was riddled with fraud.

He's repeatedly lashed out, including dropping the f-word on a Time magazine interviewer last week and angrily defending his poll numbers to a CNN reporter on Monday.

He has taken to blaming the GOP's problems on poor messaging (although not from himself).

He's spent time campaigning in a series of very red states: Alabama (which he won by 31 points in 2024), Oklahoma (Trump +34) and Nebraska (Trump +20) — the last of which he visited on Monday.

And on Monday night, he attacked the Democratic Senate nominee in another state that shouldn't be on the map: South Carolina (Trump +18). He used an anti-transgender slur to go after Democrat Annie Andrews, who's giving Sen. Darline Graham — whose appointment Trump pushed for — a tougher-than-expected race.

The GOP was already playing defense in five states Trump won by between 11 and 16 points, with the most recent addition being Kansas — a state Trump won by 16 points two years ago and that hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1932 .

But adding Nebraska and especially South Carolina to the mix is particularly striking.

And in case you thought Trump's comments about South Carolina weren't strategic, the GOP is sending $5 million to the Palmetto State to shore up Graham. Trump allies have also told CNN they are worried about the senator's polling.

One of the most telling signs of broader GOP panic? Republicans feeling compelled to distance themselves from Trump even in these red areas — whether calling for an end to the Iran war, overhauling their websites to erase mentions of the president, or declining to campaign with Trump.

On Monday, the Houston Chronicle reported that Texas Gov. Greg Abbott won't appear with Trump when the president visits San Antonio this week. Abbott's campaign blamed scheduling conflicts, but these are the kinds of events GOP candidates would never have missed once upon a time, especially in a red state.

And indeed, many of the worst signs for the GOP are emanating from Texas.

There's the awkward ad from Senate nominee Ken Paxton's estranged wife (who has accused him of infidelity) in which she encourages people to vote Republican. There are the leaked audio clips in which Paxton is heard complaining about Trump and the national GOP hurting his campaign. And on Monday, GOP state Rep. Briscoe Cain posted on X: " If the election were held tomorrow, all state wide races go blue ."

Just to underscore how stunning that would be, Democrats haven't won any statewide race in Texas since 1994. And this isn't some moderate Republican spouting off; this is a MAGA lawmaker who tried to help overturn the results of the 2020 election for Trump.

None of this means the GOP is doomed. While there are enough signs in the polling to cause the party to worry, Democrats' path to the Senate majority still goes through those double-digit Trump states. That's a high bar to clear.

And, we've seen before how parties can spend late money in lower-tier races that don't wind up being particularly close. Back in 2020, Democrats spent some real money in Kansas , and the GOP sent money to bolster South Carolina ; Republicans wound up winning those states by 11 and 10 points, respectively. Even some Democrats are pretty circumspect about their chances in South Carolina this year.

But the increased desperation ahead of November 3 means it could be a long four weeks for the GOP.

articles.title: Trump admin blocks Democratic Gov. Wes Moore from speaking at Maryland shipbuilding event
articles.summary: Democratic Gov. Wes Moore said President Donald Trump blocked him from speaking at a Tuesday event near Baltimore meant to unveil a new multi-billion-dollar...
articles.body:
Democratic Gov. Wes Moore said President Donald Trump blocked him from speaking at a Tuesday event near Baltimore meant to unveil a new multi-billion-dollar investment in submarine manufacturing.

A White House official did not dispute the account.

Moore played a role in negotiating the deal, which involved bringing the defense tech firm Anduril to a former steel plant on the Patapsco River to make components for Virginia-class submarines. The Navy is awarding the firm a $2.9 billion contract.

Trump is planning to visit the facility and give a speech on the investment Tuesday afternoon. But Moore and other Maryland Democrats won't be in attendance after the administration blocked the governor from speaking.

"If the president of the United States wants to bring the circus in town and tell me that I'm not allowed to speak, despite the fact we were the ones that helped bring the deal, then I will let the circus be conducted while I go back to the work of the people of Maryland," Moore told reporters Tuesday.

A White House official said Trump had "graciously" invited Moore to the unveiling event, but only as a guest.

"It's unfortunate that the Governor is now making a multi-billion dollar announcement about himself by throwing a tantrum over a federal initiative that will bring sorely needed jobs back to his state thanks to President Trump," the official said.

A spokesman for Moore said the governor "has always said he will work with anyone when it comes to delivering for Marylanders but bow to no one when it comes to standing up for them."

"The Governor is proud to welcome Anduril to Baltimore County and the thousands of permanent jobs this investment is bringing to our state," the spokesman said.

Speaking in the pre-program ahead of Trump's remarks, co-founder and CEO of Anduril Industries Brian Schimpf thanked several people who helped make the announcement possible, including Moore, Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Baltimore County Executive Kathy Klausmeier.

"Gov. Moore, County Executive Klausmeier, the federal congressional delegation, as well as state and local leaders throughout Maryland have all moved with urgency to help bring industrial investment at this scale to Baltimore County," Schimpf said. "They've also worked closely with us across the many requirements necessary to make this investment come to fruition."

Trump and Moore have had an acrimonious history — the president tried to bar the Democrat from a governors dinner at the White House last year. Moore is considered a potential 2028 presidential candidate.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

CNN's Kit Maher contributed to this report.

articles.title: Texas voters get ‘Are you white?’ political texts targeting James Talarico
articles.summary: The messages direct recipients to a site paid for by the American Political Action Committee, whose website identifies longtime conservative Alan Gottlieb as its founder.
articles.body: Several viewers reached out to NBC Dallas-Fort Worth after receiving text messages asking them, “Are you white?” The messages then claim James Talarico called white men “America’s top terror threat” and direct recipients to a political attack website paid for by the American Political Action Committee. The text messages and attack site refer to a comment made by Talarico after a mass shooting in which he said, “Radicalized white men are the greatest domestic terrorist threat in our country.” Talarico was referring to a Department of Homeland Security report released during the first Trump administration that described white supremacist extremists as the “most persistent and lethal” threat among domestic violent extremists. Talarico ally Rep. Marc Veasey, D-Fort Worth, described the texts as a throwback to the racial politics of the 1980s and 1990s. Veasey said he believes the messages are an effort to appeal to voters who are frustrated over issues including the war and high prices. “They’re upset about the war, they’re upset about these high prices,” Veasey said. SMU political science professor Matthew Wilson said the texts are likely to be just the beginning as outside groups pour money into the competitive U.S. Senate race. “You’re seeing people increasingly spend across state lines and try to shape the balance of power, in whichever races they think are most hotly contested and most potentially winnable,” Wilson said. As for the American Political Action Committee, or AMERIPAC, Federal Election Commission records show the Bellevue, Washington-based group has been registered with the agency since 1980. The group’s website identifies longtime conservative and Second Amendment advocate Alan Gottlieb as its founder. NBC Dallas-Fort Worth reached out to Gottlieb and the group’s treasurer for comment and has not heard back. A key to understanding these messages is the 2010 Supreme Court ruling in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, which allowed corporations and unions to spend unlimited amounts advocating for or against candidates, as long as that spending is independent of the candidates’ campaigns. The messages are an example of independent political spending, which allows outside groups to spend money advocating for or against candidates without coordinating with their campaigns. The 2010 Supreme Court ruling in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission expanded the ability of corporations and unions to fund that kind of political speech.

articles.title: Trump’s comment about Iran nuking Los Angeles and San Diego was incoherent, not malicious
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says many bizarre and even hateful things. But signaling he would allow Iran to nuke Los Angeles and San Diego is not one of them.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump says many bizarre and even hateful things. But signaling he would allow Iran to nuke Los Angeles and San Diego is not one of them.

During a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, Trump " weaved " his way right into a controversy that had critics, some in the media and even a GOP congressional candidate accusing him of rhetorically conceding major population centers on the West Coast to America's sworn enemy. And you could be forgiven for reading the president's comments that way.

But context and recent history make clear that Trump's crime was less indifference to the fate of Californians and more his increasingly profound incoherence.

Which, to be clear, is still a major problem for the most powerful man in the world.

"They can take out a city," he said of Iran . "Let them take – let it – let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That's – this is a very small price to pay."

It wouldn't be totally out of character for this to be another Trumpian verbal excess, given his recent past. This is a president who has repeatedly spoken about withholding disaster aid from states that vote against his party, and he has demonstrated some indifference to blue states . His Energy Department recently admitted in court that it canceled clean energy grants " based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state ."

Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont accused Trump of saying the small price to pay was the "annihilation of two major American cities." Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut called it " such a sick, evil thing to say ." Even GOP congressional candidate Jim Desmond, who serves on the San Diego County board of supervisors, said what Trump did was " write off American cities as an acceptable price of war ." Desmond "vehemently" disagreed with it.

But that is pretty clearly not what Trump was trying to say.

For one, immediately before the above quote, he had been talking about other costs of the Iran war — apparently referring to gas prices — being that "small price to pay."

"And again, remember — with the word — it's just artificial, it's a little bit high," Trump said. "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe."

(You can see Trump's full speech here .)

Trump didn't initially say he was referring to gas prices, mind you (though he did say that later). But this is precisely how he's been talking about them for a long time — as a "small price to pay" for preventing a nuclear Iran:

He said March 8 on Truth Social that "short term oil prices … is a very small price to pay for U.S.A., and World, Safety and Peace."

On March 16, he called high gas prices "a very small thing compared to allowing them to have" nuclear weapons.

On May 5, he called high gas prices "a very small price to pay for getting rid of a nuclear weapon."

He even said it in a separate appearance on Monday — an interview with a local Nebraska TV station : "I say it proudly: a relatively small price to pay for keeping nuclear weapons out of the hands of a lunatic nation."

Also, three days ago, Trump made a very similar argument to the one he made about Los Angeles and San Diego — except about Mobile, Alabama, during a rally there.

"But remember about the oil: You're paying a price, but boy, is that a small price than what it would be if these lunatics were allowed to have a nuclear weapon and used it on Mobile, Alabama," Trump said. "OK, not going to happen."

At his Nebraska rally, Trump basically took that talking point and made it a whole lot more unintelligible.

He bounced around from talking about Kamala Harris and the election, to wanting total victory in Iran, to talking about gas prices being high (but without actually saying "gas prices"). When he made the comment about Iran nuking Los Angeles and San Diego, he used very unfortunate sentence construction that did sound a lot like he would "let them" — Tehran, that is — nuke the two blue state cities.

And then he returned to the gas prices — but again, in an extremely confusing way.

"But it's gonna end very soon, and it'll end one way or the other, and your gas and your gasoline and all of the things —" Trump said, before jumping off on a tangent about Venezuela.

It was so confusing that not only did that GOP congressional candidate seem to interpret it in the worst way; so did many in the crowd. Indeed, the ugliest part of this whole episode is that people actually cheered when Trump floated the destruction of Los Angeles and San Diego. That would seem to say something about the movement Trump has cultivated.

But while he wasn't advocating that, his phrasing does point to a growing problem.

A president is someone you count on to be authoritative and clear, especially when talking about issues of the utmost importance like nuclear war. But Trump's rhetoric is often anything but.

Look at any recent interview where a transcript is released. Some of Trump's responses in his Time magazine interview last week , for example, are virtually impenetrable. (Just do a word search for "unintelligible" if you want some examples.) It often feels like he's engaging in a lengthy bout of free association.

Trump has long spoken like this, to an extent. And by casting his meandering soliloquies as "the weave," he's tried to make it sound intentional, allowing his supporters to believe it's his secret rhetorical genius.

But the "weave" is getting harder to follow — with potentially harmful consequences, too.

articles.title: The Memo: Trump changes course on controversial ads, underscoring midterm dangers
articles.summary: President Trump did something rare Monday evening: He climbed down. Trump announced on social media that a series of TV ads extolling his supposed strengths would no longer be paid for by the government but would instead be funded by him and his main super PAC. To be sure, Trump admitted no wrongdoing and complained…
articles.body:
President Trump did something rare Monday evening: He climbed down.

Trump announced on social media that a series of TV ads extolling his supposed strengths would no longer be paid for by the government but would instead be funded by him and his main super PAC.

To be sure, Trump admitted no wrongdoing and complained that it was only the “Radical Left” who were unhappy about the original ad buys. But the switch told a different story, suggesting the series of taxpayer-funded Trump-centric ads was playing badly with voters.

The controversy was just one more battle in a midterm war in which Trump is the central figure.

Every midterm election is in part a judgment on the president of the time. But Trump has, characteristically, inserted himself into the campaign at every possible opportunity.

He has repeatedly urged supporters to vote as if he is on the ballot. He spoke during both nights of the GOP’s unusual midterm convention in Dallas, where a succession of other speakers hailed him and his record. He is in the middle of a sprint of campaign events, which he insists can elevate his party’s fortunes.

Speaking with reporters Tuesday, Trump asserted “the rallies have changed things around” and said, “I think we’re going to do very well.”

On social media, he was even more emphatic, insisting that he was in the process of saving the GOP’s electoral skin.

In two posts Tuesday morning, he wrote that “MY RALLIES ARE SAVING THE REPUBLICAN PARTY , AGAIN!!!” and “We are flipping races all over the place.”

But Trump’s itinerary appears to reveal a different dynamic. His travel so far has taken him mostly to conservative strongholds, including Nebraska on Monday, and Alabama and Oklahoma before that.

The locations may in part be intended to ensure the president is met by the adoring crowds from which he seems to draw energy. But they are also indicative of a midterm landscape where Democrats are advancing.

Senate races that Republicans did not believe would be competitive this cycle have tightened, including in GOP redoubts like Texas and Kansas.

This is surely due in large part to Trump’s sagging approval ratings. He stands at just 38 percent approval in the current polling average from The Hill’s data and polling partner, Decision Desk HQ.

There are signs, too, of some Republicans trying to create distance from the president.

A striking example came this week when it emerged that Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) would not attend the president’s rally in San Antonio, set for Wednesday.

Abbott has ascribed the decision to a scheduling conflict, but it’s a move that raises eyebrows.

Abbott is in an unexpectedly competitive race for reelection. Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa, a Texas state representative, led him by 3 points among likely voters in a recent New York Times/Siena poll.

Previously, three GOP Senate candidates also in tough races — Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio, Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa and former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan — urged a quick end to the war on Iran, albeit without criticizing Trump directly.

When it comes to the House, Republican gloom is near-total. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) told MS NOW’s “The Beat” on Monday that “the House is almost statistically impossible to win at this point.”

Some Democrats have taken to taunting Trump. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, on Monday sardonically appealed to Trump to “come to Michigan,” during an interview with MS NOW’s Chris Hayes.

Trump’s centrality to the campaign is “very damaging” to the GOP’s chances, Julian Zelizer, professor of history and public affairs at Princeton, told this column. “Them being tied to him, him being more present, isn’t helpful.”

Zelizer cited voter discontent with the cost of living and the war on Iran as especially corrosive.

“Voters are connecting the dots between President Trump’s foreign policy, particularly Iran, and the cost of living. So when he is out there, it’s not just that he’s not dealing with the issues the public cares about. It’s reminding them of the person they blame.”

There is also Trump’s unquenchable appetite for controversy to consider.

On Monday, he sparked yet another furor with transphobic comments about the Democratic Senate nominee in South Carolina, Annie Andrews.

This comes on top of his long-running public battles over Washington landmarks from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to the Kennedy Center, and his repeated attacks on the media.

Despite it all, some Trump loyalists maintain that the naysayers are wrong.

They argue that the president has a unique capacity to turn out the MAGA base and that voters motivated by animus toward him are immovable regardless of what he does or doesn’t do.

“If you told me there are a bunch of undecided voters, then maybe [there would be a downside] but there are none,” said Barry Bennett, a senior adviser to Trump’s first campaign in 2016.

Asserting that Democrats have nothing to offer but “hot air and hate,” Bennett was also scathing of the idea that Trump’s campaign trail appearances would backfire in any concrete way.

“Someone is going to hate him more because he came to their town? I don’t see it,” he said.

Yet others contend that Trump is ultimately hurting his party because he is now so synonymous with an economy that has left voters deeply discontented.

“Donald Trump is trying to change the narrative of a failed presidency by going and doing these rallies and showing these crowds,” said Todd Belt, a professor of political management at George Washington University.

“But that is probably not going to work with a lot of independents because the economy is the number one issue.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Why Democrats may need a gut check on their midterm ambitions: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki writes that some Democrats fear the party’s election expectations are getting too rosy. Plus, Ben Kamisar dives into one big factor working in the GOP’s favor. — Adam Wollner Why Democrats may need a gut check on their midterm ambitions Analysis by Natasha Korecki Democrats have had an extraordinary run of good news with less than a month until Election Day. Polls show President Donald Trump’s approval rating in free fall amid growing angst over his handling of the economy and the Iran war. Key groups, like Latinos, are abandoning Republicans in droves. Prognosticators increasingly shifting race ratings in Democrats’ direction has spurred a litany of headlines about the potential prizes awaiting the party. Can they snag a Senate seat in Kansas? What about South Carolina? In addition to the Texas Senate contest, can Democrat Gina Hinojosa knock out Republican Gov. Greg Abbott? “I’ve been trying to tell yall: Don’t sleep on Mississippi,” the longtime Democratic strategist James Carville posted on X last week, referring to the Senate race in a state Trump carried by 23 points two years ago. As crunch time hits these campaigns, Democrats have critical questions before them: Should they reach for the stars? Or are they getting starry-eyed? We’ve all been here before. A poll-driven media cycle that paints a far rosier picture for one party (Republicans in 2022) or another (Democrats in 2024). One Democratic national strategist working on races across the country said the party needs to pump the brakes on its optimism. “The Senate is far from secure,” said the strategist, who was not authorized to comment publicly. “We should remain aggressive in Maine and Michigan, single-digit presidential states that are not yet secure organizationally.” The Democrat, who added that Alaska’s Senate race is also worth sustained investment, noted that Republicans have an enormous spending advantage in many of the contests that will determine which party wins the majority. (More on that below.) There are other reasons Democrats should proceed with caution. While Latino voters are swinging away from Republicans, there are still big questions around whether they will turn out for the other side. That goes for other critical voting blocs, too. Despite deep dissatisfaction with Trump, as well as notable energy on the left this year, the Democratic Party as a whole is still receiving low marks. And as polling shows depressed Republicans may sit it out, there’s also a pivotal group of undecided voters who in the end could come back to the GOP, particularly in red states. Still, it is Republicans who are on the defensive with four weeks to go. Last week, a top GOP super PAC canceled its remaining ad buys in the North Carolina Senate race, a sign that Democrats are on track to flip the seat. The group, Senate Leadership Fund, has also begun directing money to Senate contests in deep-red Kansas and South Carolina. And if Democrat James Talarico weren’t a threat, Republicans wouldn’t have, in September alone, dumped $122 million into a state Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024. “It’s a toss-up race right now. It’s 50-50,” a Republican working on Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign said. But the bottom line is to win the Senate, Democrats need a net gain of four seats, including at least two that Trump won by double-digits in 2024. And they’d need to stretch even further into Trump territory if they aren’t able to unseat longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins in Maine or defend seats in battlegrounds like Michigan and New Hampshire. The Democratic strategist put it succinctly: “We should sleep on Mississippi.” ☀️ Related read: Florida Democrats try to regain their mojo after years of Republican dominance, by Matt Dixon Republicans fight red-state midterm chaos with hundreds of millions in late money By Ben Kamisar Republicans are swamping House and Senate races with an unprecedented flood of late ad spending as the party tests whether hundreds of millions of dollars can buy it some reprieve from the eroding political environment that’s threatening longtime GOP states and districts. Since the start of September, Republicans have made more than $700 million worth of new advertising bookings in congressional races alone, according to an NBC News analysis of data from AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm. That’s new money on top of what had already been committed to those races in ad reservations made over the summer. By comparison, Democrats booked more than $430 million in new ad reservations across those races last month. The disparity is greatest in the battle for the Senate majority, where almost 7 of every 10 newly booked advertising dollars are coming from Republicans. The gap is smaller in the House, where a bit less than 6 in 10 of those new ad dollars are coming from the GOP. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
