articles.title: Collins, Jackson clash in first Maine Senate debate: 4 takeaways
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson faced off Tuesday in the first debate of their neck-and-neck Senate race in Maine. A rare Republican to win statewide in blue-leaning Maine, five-term Collins used the debate stage to spotlight times she’s bucked her party, from her pro-choice position to her vote against President Trump’s signature…
articles.body:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson faced off Tuesday in the first debate of their neck-and-neck Senate race in Maine.

A rare Republican to win statewide in blue-leaning Maine, five-term Collins used the debate stage to spotlight times she’s bucked her party, from her pro-choice position to her vote against President Trump’s signature “Big Beautiful Bill” — while Jackson, a former president of the state Senate, tied Collins to Trump’s agenda and hammered her controversial vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.

The candidates also sparred over immigration, healthcare and abortion rights in the hourlong WGME program as polls indicate a tight race that could reshape Maine politics.

Jackson became the party’s pick to take on Collins this fall after Graham Platner, a progressive who won the party’s initial primary, withdrew amid sexual misconduct allegations. Despite a shortened campaign runway, Jackson has been leading Collins by roughly a point in Decision Desk HQ’s polling averages of the race, and top forecasters rate the race a critical toss-up in the fight for Senate control.

The rivals are expected to face off in three more debates over the next two weeks, with the next set for Thursday.

Here are three takeaways from their first showdown:

Jackson presses Collins on Kavanaugh vote

Collins was reelected in 2014 by nearly 40 points, but notched another term by a comparatively narrow 9 points in 2020 after Democrats in the state were outraged by her 2018 vote to confirm Kavanaugh to the nation’s highest court.

On Tuesday, Jackson sought to connect Collins’s vote to Kavanaugh’s role in the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision to overturn abortion rights in Roe v. Wade.

“Maine women, I know many of them came to your office and begged you not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but you did it anyways. And then he overturned Roe, and you still say that you don’t regret that vote. So I guess what I’m curious about is what will it take for you to admit that you were wrong, you know, especially whenever Kavanaugh went out and did what he did?” Jackson asked his debate stage rival.

Collins said she looks at justice nominees for “whether they’re fit to serve on the court” rather than trying to predict how he or she would vote on any issue.

“I clearly don’t agree with how Brett Kavanaugh voted on Roe v. Wade,” Collins said, noting that she also voted for Democrat-nominated Justices Sonya Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Katanji Brown Jackson.

Collins has said that Kavanaugh told her before his confirmation that he considered Roe v. Wade “settled law,” but when pressed about their exchange on the debate stage, she denied feeling that he lied to her.

“I do not feel that he lied, but I think that he should not have said it was settled law because, to me, that meant that it would not be overturned. But to be fair, you cannot ask a nominee how he might vote on some hypothetical future case.”

Meanwhile, Collins knocked Jackson for taking a more conservative stance on abortion earlier in his career, saying “there’s only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice.” She also chided Jackson over Maine’s high cost of living, pointing to state policies during his 20-year tenure in the Legislature.

Collins distances from Trump: ‘I’m not exactly his favorite’

As she fights for a sixth term in blue Maine, Collins kept her party’s leaders and legislative moves at arm’s length, despite claims from Jackson and other Democrats that she’s sided with Trump 96 percent of the time.

Collins called that number “greatly misleading” and argued that the same study found “I voted against my party more than any other senator on either side of the aisle.”

When Jackson jabbed early at her vote to advance Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” out of committee, she argued that the vote was necessary to advance other legislative agenda items and stressed that she ultimately sided against the final passage.

Jackson, though, took issue with that framing, calling Collins an “arsonist who helped set the fire, and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out.”

The incumbent also stressed her pro-choice position, a rare move for a Republican Senate hopeful, and said the war in Iran was “not well thought out.” And she deflected on whether she’d stand by Trump if he were to visit Maine as he crisscrosses red states to boost some of the party’s most vulnerable candidates.

“I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she said. “I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”

Rivals diverge on ICE after fatal Maine shooting

Collins and Jackson diverged on their approach to Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after Johan Duran Guerrero was shot and killed by a federal immigration in Biddeford, Maine, earlier this year.

The incident has put Collins on the defensive as Democrats seek to tie her to Trump and his unpopular immigration crackdown. After the July shooting, protestors surged on the Republican’s office in Biddeford with calls to “vote her out.”

“It’s time that ICE is disbanded, and we go back to putting that money in the Customs and Border Patrol. They have training. They’re law enforcement. People respect them. We don’t respect ICE,” Jackson said on Tuesday’s debate stage.

But while Collins called the shooting “horrific,” she argued that ICE “needs further reform” rather than a total cut.

“You cannot abolish ICE. It does need reform, but you really want to abolish an agency that is responsible for deporting violent criminals?” she asked, noting her support for body-worn cameras and other changes to agency practices.

Candidates tackle tariffs, economic strain on Maine

Jackson and Collins quickly went viral for an exchange over road salt as they tackled the president’s tariffs and talked economic strains on the Pine Tree State.

Collins reiterated her opposition to Trump’s tariffs on Canada, stressing that America’s longtime ally to the north is a vital trading partner for the northeastern state in particular.

“But I’ve also been working behind the scenes. Troy [Jackson] mocked it, but I was successful in getting concrete, pulp, and road salt removed from the tariff list. And if you ask towns in northern Maine and eastern Maine, they get all of their road salt from Canada,” the senator said.

“I didn’t mock the fact that she got road salt back. I mock the fact that: what about everything else? I mean, we can’t eat road salt,” Jackson hit back.

The Democrat added that, in light of the Iran war and other factors driving up prices, “there’s going to be so many less people to be able to afford to drive that I’m not even sure the road salt’s going to be worth anything either.”

At different points in the night, the pair cast blame on each other for Maine’s economic struggles.

Jackson pointed to Collins’s votes in Washington, while Collins pointed to state policies during Jackson’s 20-year tenure in the Legislature.

articles.title: Republican John James seeks some distance from Trump in Michigan governor debate
articles.summary: Republican Rep. John James on Tuesday sought to put some daylight between himself and President Donald Trump as he debated his opponent in the Michigan governor’s race.
articles.body: Republican Rep. John James on Tuesday sought to put some daylight between himself and President Donald Trump as he debated his opponent in the Michigan governor’s race. Democratic nominee Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, repeatedly attempted to tie James to Trump during the hourlong showdown, saying the congressman had failed to stand up to the president and wouldn’t do so as governor, either. James, who was boosted by Trump’s endorsement in his GOP primary campaign, pointed to the Iran War and tariff policy as issues where he has disagreements with the president. “I’ve stood up to the president many times. I’ve said that I can agree with the president without worshiping him. I can disagree without attacking him, and I always put Michigan first,” James said. James said he believed the conflict in Iran needed to end “quickly, as in yesterday,” echoing comments he made last month. James, who has voted against several resolutions in the House that attempt to end the Iran war, also said that he wants to “use whatever checks and balance power that we have to bring this war to a swift conclusion.” His comments in his first debate with Benson in the key battleground state come as polls show voters nationally continuing to sour on Trump’s handling of the Iran war and the cost of living as the midterm elections draw closer. Benson attacked James for voting against the Iran war powers resolutions, while blaming high gas prices on the conflict. “I struggle with that vote,” James said of the war powers resolutions votes. “I’m a combat veteran. I have been to war. She has not. I understand what war means, and so I voted to protect the troops and to fund them while they were in harm’s way.” Benson pointed out that her husband served in the Army. “Military spouses serve also, congressman,” she said. Benson sought to link James to Trump’s tariff agenda, saying she dubs them the “John James tax,” while James said he had pushed back on the Trump administration’s tariffs against Canada. “I’ve actually called out the administration specifically, talking with the trade ambassador and saying that we must get back to the table, stop acting like children, and negotiate a reciprocal, fair, and mutually beneficial arrangement to make sure that we can bring our jobs back and protect our industry,” James said. James, who in July promised to “back law enforcement, end sanctuary city policies,” and “cooperate with federal immigration authorities to remove criminal illegal immigrants,” on Tuesday seemed to soften that stance, saying that he does not see a need for ICE presence in Michigan. “We’re going to be cooperating with federal law enforcement as well as our communities. We’re going to make sure that we’re prioritizing violent offenders, and we’re going to make sure that we enforce the law,” James said. “Frankly, I don’t believe we’re going to need ICE presence in the state of Michigan because we are going to be enforcing the law.” James attempted to tie Benson’s record to that of term-limited Democratic Governor Gretchen Whitmer. Asked by moderator Rick Albin from the local TV station WOOD-TV to point to a decision where Whitmer did not listen to Michiganders, Benson did not cite a specific policy, but said “where I think we need to listen to the people and is a way to improve our Department of Health and Human Services.” The candidates also clashed on data centers amid a growing public backlash to them, with both accusing the other of profiting from them. Benson accused James of voting for policies friendly to data centers while holding stocks in them, and James accused Benson’s family of profiting from one center’s construction. Benson denied that her family had profited from them, while James said that any data center-related stocks he owns were held in broad mutual funds. The nationally watched Michigan Senate race, in which the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed is running against former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, did not come up during Tuesday’s gubernatorial debate. Republicans in particular have been eager to tie El-Sayed, a progressive, to other Democratic candidates in competitive races. Neither candidate mentioned that race, or attempted to tie their opponent with either Senate nominee. Democrats are looking to keep Michigan’s governorship in their party’s hands after Whitmer’s two terms in office. Trump carried the state by just over 1 point in the 2024 presidential election. NBC News characterizes the race as leaning towards Democrats. Benson and James are scheduled to debate again on Oct. 15.

articles.title: Fuel industry warns truck stops not to sell red dye diesel after Trump lifts restrictions
articles.summary: “We do not expect most reputable diesel retailers and fuel marketers to do this,” said several industry groups. “There’s limited upside.”
articles.body:
Truck stops nationwide were warned to "proceed with caution" Tuesday by a major industry group after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to promote the use of "red dye" diesel fuel.

Red dye diesel is exempt from federal excise taxes because it is intended for farm equipment and other off-road uses.

The order, signed before farmers in Nebraska on Monday night, aims to bring down fuel prices by "temporarily" allowing highway use of red dye diesel fuel, according to a White House statement .

U.S. voters are deeply frustrated by the high price of gas, and the Trump administration is under intense pressure to bring down fuel costs before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Monday's order instructs Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to "defer certain diesel fuel tax payment obligations and to provide penalty relief to the extent permitted by law."

It does not waive the federal taxes, because only Congress can eliminate a tax.

Following Trump's directive, the Energy Marketers of America warned gas stations to "proceed with caution."

"Whether relief is available, whom it covers, and on what conditions depend on Treasury determinations and guidance not yet issued," the group said. "Deferral is not forgiveness."

Moreover, the order does not "resolve EPA or state restrictions" on the dyed variety of diesel fuel, the EMA said.

Other trucking and gas industry groups sounded a similar note of caution.

"The White House appears to be trying to encourage the supply chain to move toward selling dyed fuel in non-traditional ways," the Society of Independent Gasoline Marketers of America and the National Association of Truck Stop Owners said in a note to their members.

"We do not expect most reputable diesel retailers and fuel marketers to do this," they said. "First, the tax is still owed, so there's limited upside."

In addition, "the logistical challenges outweigh any visible upside: Residual dye lingers in tanks and fuel systems."

For most fuel sellers, "the liability and customer risk outweigh any temporary, uncertain benefit."

The White House did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

A group representing independent long-haul truckers also suggested Trump's move would provide little benefit to its members.

"Allowing the wider use of red-dyed diesel will provide minimal relief. Market stability is essential to bring down costs for the long haul," said Todd Spencer, president of the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association.

Since the war with Iran began, the price of diesel has surged from $3.76 per gallon to $6.32 as of Tuesday, a nearly 70% increase.

The Iran conflict is not the only conflict contributing to diesel's skyrocketing price.

A recent escalation of the Ukraine-Russia war has included strikes by Ukrainian drones on Russian refineries.

Russia, traditionally one of the world's large diesel exporters, has responded to the attacks by imposing a diesel export ban through at least the end of October.

Trump has urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russia's diesel infrastructure .

"Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump told reporters in early September . "There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel, because that's hurting the world."

Oil prices also remain sharply elevated since the beginning of the year. Brent crude oil, which traded Tuesday night above $101 per barrel, is up more than 66% since the start of the year.

images.caption: Despite an executive order promoting red dye diesel, trucking and fuel industry groups are warning their members it may not be worth the risk. (Clayton Steward / Bloomberg via Getty)

articles.title: Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson: 5 takeaways from Maine Senate debate
articles.summary: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson clashed over President Trump and their records in first debate for Senate seat that could decide control of Congress.
articles.body:
Five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson clashed over President Donald Trump and their records in the first debate for the Maine U.S. Senate seat that could decide which party takes power in Washington.

The race is being closely watched nationally as it could determine control of the Senate , which is narrowly held by Republicans, 53-47. Recent polls have shown a tight race: a University of New Hampshire poll from mid-September found Jackson ahead by 4 percentage points , while a New York Times/Siena University poll from a similar time period found Collins ahead by 3 percentage points .

It's also been a race mired in scandal. Jackson, the former Maine Senate President, replaced oyster farmer Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee in July following a sexual assault allegation that Platner denies. Collins and Jackson have also both faced accusations of misconduct against their campaigns in recent weeks.

The candidates responded to these accusations and discussed a wide range of issues, from affordability to their records to Trump, in the debate broadcast on WGME . Here are five takeaways.

See Susan Collins, Troy Jackson and more campaign in Maine midterms

Troy Jackson speaks as he became the Maine Democratic Party's choice to be their U.S. Senate nominee to replace Graham Platner on the ballot in November on July 25, 2026, in Bangor, Maine. Troy Jackson will face off against Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, in the general election.

Jackson sought to tie Collins to Trump throughout the debate, repeatedly saying that Collins has voted with Trump 96% of the time and that her Republican colleagues have called her a "team player." He criticized Collins for advancing the One Big Beautiful Bill out of committee, voting to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court and voting for a $70 billion funding package for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Collins, on the other hand, tried to distance herself from the president. She argued that the 96% is too high and based on only one study, while another found her voting with Trump only 72% of the time. She said that she has consistently voted against her party and that she ultimately voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill. She also highlighted other areas where she has broken with Trump, such as voting to end the war in Iran and against the tariffs in Canada.

Collins has long had a reputation as a moderate Republican, but it's been difficult to thread the needle in the Trump era. The president has floated a visit to Maine, and when asked if she would "stand with him" if he does, she didn't give a yes or no answer.

"I don't think that President Trump is going to come to Maine. He's talking about going to a lot of different states," Collins said. "I've heard nothing from his office, and I'm not exactly his favorite senator ."

Collins has long been known as someone who "brings home the bacon" to Maine, a term that means she secures federal dollars for her state. She brought it up immediately in her opening statement.

"In the past four years, I've secured $1.5 billion for 672 projects, from Madawaska to Kittery, from Eastport to Rumford," Collins said.

She also frequently cited specific policies she helped author, like a $50 billion fund to help rural healthcare and the Paycheck Protection Program, which she said saved 250,000 jobs in Maine.

This strategy of "pork barrel politics" and specific policy details is a time-honored one among incumbent politicians, but it has lately fallen by the wayside as newcomers campaign in more flashy ways. Collins may be hoping that emphasizing her loyalty to Maine will help her to overcome national headwinds against Republicans.

However, Jackson argued that the money she brings back pales in comparison to the money lost by Trump's policies. He said that Collins "is like an arsonist who helps set the fire, and she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out."

Jackson said he made sure to pass progressive policies in the state Senate like lowering prescription drug and universal school meals, although he provided limited details on specific legislation.

Similarly, Collins stressed her bipartisanship and ability to get things done in Congress, areas where she said Jackson might struggle. She attacked him for not being able to get bills passed when serving in the state house.

"How do you think you're going to get things done in a mostly divided Senate as the most junior senator?" she asked. "To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships."

Jackson responded that Collins doesn't understand the legislative process in Maine and that some bills must be discarded to make progress. He suggested that what she is getting passed isn't aligned with Mainer's priorities.

"Senator Collins is saying that she's been passing more bills in Congress. I mean, I don't see it," Jackson said. "I certainly don't think that, you know, a lot of the ones that she has been fighting for has been helping us."

Collins and Jackson have faced various accusations in recent weeks. On Sept. 22, ProPublica reported that the FBI had ended an investigation into allegations that a fundraiser for Collins had participated in an illegal campaign donation scheme after the Trump administration purged the Justice Department and FBI of its teams that handle public corruption cases.

Collins called the allegations "completely false" and "very offensive."

Jackson has faced an attack from a GOP ad that accuses him of abusing his power when he was state Senate president to help out his lobbyist son. Jackson said that independent fact checkers have proved "that there was nothing there."

Collins also attacked Jackson for claiming a Federal Housing Authority loan on his Allagash home, which he claimed was his primary residence when he was living part-time in Augusta as state Senate president. However, the Maine Ethics Commission voted against investigating Jackson at the time, saying he had not violated campaign finance law.

Whose fault is it — Washington's or Maine's?

Both candidates agreed that families are struggling in Maine. But they disagreed on the cause. Collins argued that Maine's high electricity rates, housing costs and property taxes are due to failures at the state house level, while Jackson blamed policies passed under the Trump administration in Washington, including the Iran war and the One Big Beautiful Bill.

articles.title: Georgia governor candidates spar over the economy and Trump in lone debate
articles.summary: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson clashed Tuesday night during their only scheduled debate of this fall’s race for governor in Georgia.
articles.body: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson clashed Tuesday night during their only scheduled debate of this fall’s race for governor in Georgia, taking aim at each other on economic issues, data centers and President Donald Trump. Public polls show Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta and a former Biden administration official, and Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive, locked in a close race four weeks out from Election Day, with early voting kicking off next week. The hourlong, town-hall-style debate was largely civil, featuring live and taped questions from voters. Jackson frequently ripped his opponent over her record as mayor, while Bottoms attacked his praise of Trump. “My opponent has said he wants to be Trump’s favorite governor. He wants to be Trump with a Southern tone. He said there’s not a single policy that he disagrees with Trump on,” Bottoms said in response to a question about the Trump administration’s cuts to federal funding. “I will stand up to Donald Trump when necessary. I’m not running to be his favorite governor,” she continued. Jackson responded, “I don’t owe anybody anything,” and said, “Nobody’s ever told me what to do.” He then invoked Brian Kemp, Georgia’s popular, term-limited governor — the first of multiple times he did so. “I will stand up to anybody, just like Brian Kemp has done. He works with both parties, both presidents, and he stands up when he disagrees,” Jackson said. Trump endorsed Jackson’s rival, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, during the Republican gubernatorial primary. But Jackson still attempted to claim the MAGA mantle and leaned heavily into comparing himself to the president. Since winning the nomination in June, he’s backed off that approach and sought to link himself more to Kemp, who had also backed Jones. Jackson took several shots at Bottoms over her tenure as mayor, accusing her of being responsible for regional inflation in the Atlanta area that he claimed exceeded national inflation rates and pointing to higher crime rates in the city during the Covid-19 pandemic. “This is the kind of policy that we cannot have in running Georgia, not having people feeling safe to go to work,” Jackson said. “Bad mayors don’t make good governors.” While the candidates were asked about housing and education, the event focused predominantly on economic issues and affordability, with both candidates repeatedly pressed about how they’d bring down costs. Both focused heavily on tax relief. Bottoms emphasized her proposals to cut or suspend state or local taxes on a raft of items, like auto insurance, groceries, hygiene products and diapers. Jackson reiterated his promise to cut state income taxes, property taxes and taxes on certain utilities. Data centers and the controversial surveillance traffic cameras known as Flock cameras also took center stage. On data centers, Bottoms repeated her desire to implement a pause on new construction. Jackson said he wouldn’t approve new construction as governor without first getting local community approval, establishing environmental standards and getting a commitment that local communities’ power bills would be reduced. But the two sparred over the issue, as well, with Bottoms accusing Jackson of investing in data centers and Jackson accusing her of having approved building them as mayor. Bottoms also said she wasn’t opposed to a moratorium on installing new Flock cameras, while Jackson said he was. The issue of election security — which has hung over Georgia politics for six years — also came up. Bottoms said she was “deeply concerned about Donald Trump’s rhetoric around our elections.” Jackson, however, when he was asked whether he thought the U.S. Justice Department should be “overseeing and getting involved” in the state’s elections, deferred to Kemp again. “I don’t think that’s necessary unless Gov. Kemp thinks it’s necessary,” he said. Jackson has flooded the airwaves with ads, using tens of millions of dollars of his own money to outspend Bottoms 7-to-1 as of last week. That disparity has worried many Democrats, who’ve seen this year as a prime opportunity to flip the governorship blue for the first time in 16 years. Aiding Bottoms is the broader political environment in Georgia and nationally: Trump faces negative approval ratings and voter concerns about his administration’s handling of the economy.

articles.title: Zach Lahn’s residency history and Rob Sand’s party come under fire in first Iowa governor debate
articles.summary: Lahn, the Republican nominee, and Sand, the Democratic state auditor, are running to succeed retiring GOP Gov. Kim Reynolds.
articles.body: Republican Zach Lahn and Democrat Rob Sand repeatedly returned to one topic in their first debate Tuesday night in the race to be Iowa’s next governor: questions about Lahn’s residency history in the state. Sand, the state auditor, and Lahn, a businessman, met in Davenport as they run to succeed retiring Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds in an unusually competitive race for a state that has trended to the right in recent years. Iowa has not had a Democrat in the governor’s mansion since Chet Culver was defeated in 2010, and Sand is the only Democrat currently elected statewide. While Sand has cast himself as an independent-minded candidate, Lahn labeled him a “radical liberal” and a “career politician” who supports liberal positions on taxes and immigration. As the two men sparred over tax rates, economic growth, addressing the state’s cancer crisis and other issues on NBC affiliate KWQC, both repeatedly referred to the controversy over Lahn’s reported ties to Kansas, which include public records showing he voted there in 2018, 2020 and 2022 before he registered in Iowa in 2024. Lahn responded Tuesday to reports that he still frequently flies to a second home in Kansas. “I’m a sixth-generation Iowan. I live in Iowa today. I have lived in Iowa. Rob has been lying about this, and the issue is I have a blended family, and my kids split time,” he said. The subject first arose in a conversation about education. Sand advocated for increasing teacher salaries and better oversight of the use of public funding, while Lahn called for stronger auditing of the school voucher system and limiting the program to lower-income families. “I want to be the biggest advocate for public school kids in the state,” Lahn said. Sand responded: “I don’t think you’re going to be the biggest advocate for public school students over a guy who sends his kids there. When you were running advertisements saying that Marxists have hijacked the curriculum in Iowa, Zach, I’m pretty sure that that’s just more evidence that you don’t spend enough time in Iowa.” Lahn called the attacks “the central lie of Rob Sand’s campaign.” The controversy has been a drag on Lahn’s campaign, with Sand holding an advantage in public polling ahead of November’s election. Throughout the debate, Lahn lambasted Sand as a “liberal billionaire” backed by his wife’s family’s money. Sand’s wife, Christine, is the CEO of her family’s company, the Lauridsen Group, which owns several food and health product companies. Her family has donated more than $12 million to Sand’s campaigns over the years, having backed him since he first ran for state auditor. Earlier in the night, the candidates were asked how they would address Iowa’s low economic growth rate and the question of affordability on Day 1 in office. Lahn said he would prioritize homegrown businesses and make sure state government was “not prioritizing big out-of-state projects that are not employing people, like data centers.” He did indicate he would support tax incentives for the White House-backed $15 billion steel mill project announced last week. He also praised President Donald Trump’s executive action loosening restrictions on tax-exempt “red dye diesel” fuel used for farm vehicles, which he said he proposed to Vice President JD Vance when he visited Iowa last month. The rising cost of diesel, now $6.05 per gallon in Iowa, has been a major concern for farmers in the state, who have also felt the squeeze from rising fertilizer prices and tariffs, threatening the campaigns of GOP candidates in the heartland. Sand called for a cap on utility fees, ending the privatization of Medicaid in Iowa, raising the minimum wage — which he has said should be set at $12 an hour — and importing prescription drugs from Canada. Lahn wouldn’t commit to raise the minimum wage, which was last raised in Iowa in 2009 and is at $7.25 an hour. He said he would focus on industry deconsolidation and lowering taxes. “We’ve had some great efforts to lower taxes for the people of Iowa, and Rob, you’ve opposed those efforts at every step,” Lahn shot at his opponent. “And so I think we have to be very honest here about where we’re standing. Rob is supporting the raising of taxes because that’s what liberals do: They want to raise taxes. I’m here to cut taxes.” Asked to respond, Sand denied that he wants to raise taxes. Both candidates made a point to address cancer rates in their opening statements. Iowa is one of three states where the incidence of cancer is increasing amid environmental risks associated with chemicals used by the agriculture industry, like glyphosate, PFAS and nitrates. “Iowa is at a point where we are at the bottom for economic growth; we’re at the top for cancer growth,” Sand said. Lahn cited “the fastest rate of new cancer in the country” as one of three issues that motivated him to run for office. Lahn, who is backed by prominent members of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, has made cancer rates a centerpiece of his campaign, frequently targeting the powerful agriculture industry. He called addressing cancer a “foundational question” and the “crisis of our generation.” “For a very long time, we have seen the nitrate load in our water increase year after year,” he said. “We have to start to put in place real solutions.” He voiced support for the state’s IWiLL program (Iowa’s Water and Land Legacy) to address water quality issues and high nitrate levels. “I’m glad that Mr. Lahn brought up IWiLL and mentioned that he’s been supporting it and talking about it since he started the campaign. I’m glad that he’s been doing that,” Sand said. “I actually voted for it in 2010 because I lived here. You didn’t.”

articles.title: Benson, James spar in Michigan gubernatorial debate: 3 takeaways
articles.summary: Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D) and Rep. John James (R-Mich.) faced off on the debate stage Tuesday, less than a month before voters decide which of the two will be the Wolverine State’s next governor. During the debate, which Nexstar’s WOOD-TV hosted, the candidates touched on issues specific to the state — such…
articles.body:
Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D) and Rep. John James (R-Mich.) faced off on the debate stage Tuesday, less than a month before voters decide which of the two will be the Wolverine State’s next governor.

During the debate, which Nexstar’s WOOD-TV hosted, the candidates touched on issues specific to the state — such as when Benson vowed to improve the efficiency of the Michigan Department and Health and Human Services and James pledged to cut taxes.

But national and international issues were also topics of conversation on Tuesday, including President Trump’s tariff war with Canada and the Iran conflict .

Here are three takeaways from the hour-long debate between the two candidates battling to succeed term-limited Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D).

Benson, James back suspending federal gas tax

Both candidates backed suspending the federal gas tax, as Michiganders face high prices at the pump amid the Iran war.

“My opponent could go, as I’ve asked him and others to do, to Washington tomorrow and eliminate or put a holiday on the federal gas tax, which would also provide necessary relief for Michigan families and families all across this nation,” Benson remarked.

“I have called on both the suspension of the federal and the state gas tax,” James said later in the debate.

A gallon of regular gas costs roughly $4.43 on average in Michigan as of Wednesday, above the national average of about $4.37 per gallon, according to data from AAA. Diesel fuel costs nearly $6.60 per gallon in the state, almost 30 cents higher than the national average.

In backing a suspension of the state fuel tax of roughly 52 cents per gallon, James noted such a move could lead to Michigan gas prices falling below $4 on average. But analysts have told The Hill that gas stations may not pass off the entire suspended gas tax to consumers.

Benson noted she was “open” to suspending the state fuel tax, while saying the federal government must “take responsibility” for elevated prices amid the war.

“I’m always open to finding any way to reduce costs as well, here in Michigan, and I’m looking forward to having those conversations with folks on both sides of the aisle in [the state capital,] Lansing,” the Democrat said.

James urges U.S., Canadian officials to ‘stop acting like children’ amid trade war

James broke with the Trump administration regarding the president’s tariffs on Canadian imports , saying he has urged U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to return to negotiations.

“We must get back to the table, stop acting like children and negotiate a reciprocal, fair and mutually beneficial arrangement, to make sure that we can bring our jobs back and protect our industry,” the three-term representative said of what he told Greer.

James did not explicitly say whether he supported Trump’s proposed 50 percent tariffs on Canadian automobiles, set to go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Canada is Michigan’s top trading partner , as businesses in the state export $21.2 billion worth of goods to America’s northern neighbor annually, according to data from the Canadian government.

More than half of that is concentrated in the vehicles sector, including trucks, automobiles, engines and turbines.

Benson blasted Trump’s import taxes and promised to negotiate a “subnational agreement” with Canada if elected governor.

“It will enable us to ensure goods going between Michigan and Canada, and back and forth, are protected from these tariffs, from the John James tax, that has driven up costs and cost Michiganders jobs,” she added.

James says Iran war should have ended ‘yesterday’

When moderator Rick Albin asked James if there was an issue he disagreed with the president on, the congressman pointed to the seven-plus-month Iran conflict .

“Iran cannot have a nuke, but we need to wrap this thing up … yesterday,” James said, after praising the administration for exerting economic and diplomatic pressure on the Islamic Republic.

A former Army officer who served in Iraq, James said he will work with Trump to “do what we can” to end the war.

But Benson criticized her Republican opponent for voting six times against House war powers resolutions aimed at forcing the president to wind down the conflict.

“We need to be clear how we got here. It’s because of a reckless war in Iran that my opponent has voted six times to support, and that is directly to blame for the rising cost of gas and oil in this nation right now,” the Michigan secretary of state said early in the debate.

James defended his votes, saying they stemmed from his desire to keep funding the military while troops “were in harm’s way.”

articles.title: Sparks fly in first Iowa governor’s debate: 5 takeaways
articles.summary: Accusations of carpetbagging, attacks over family wealth and barbs over culture war issues dominated the first televised debate between Republican Zach Lahn and Democrat Rob Sand as the two vie to replace retiring Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) next month. Lahn and Sand participated in an hour-long debate hosted by KWQC and held at St. Ambrose…
articles.body:
Accusations of carpetbagging, attacks over family wealth and barbs over culture war issues dominated the first televised debate between Republican Zach Lahn and Democrat Rob Sand as the two vie to replace retiring Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) next month.

Lahn and Sand participated in an hour-long debate hosted by KWQC and held at St. Ambrose University in Davenport, Iowa on Tuesday, as the two make their pitch to become the next Iowa governor.

Lahn accused Sand of being a “radical liberal” who’s lied about Lahn’s family roots while Sand suggested Lahn only offered “platitudes” showing that the GOP candidate “doesn’t have the demonstrated knowledge or experience.”

Democrats believe they have a unique opportunity in Sand to win the Iowa gubernatorial race, which hasn’t been represented by a member of their party in two decades. The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates Reynolds’s seat as “lean Democrat.”

Sand and Lahn will participate in three more debates before Election Day.

Here’s 5 takeaways from the first Iowa governor’s debate:

Lobs thrown over candidates’ family backgrounds

One running theme throughout the night was the personal attacks lobbed between the two candidates over their family backgrounds and roots.

Sand hit Lahn over his ties to Kansas and suggested he wouldn’t be able to govern Iowa full-time if elected.

“You literally voted in Kansas in 2018 and in ‘20 and in ‘22. You registered to vote in Iowa less than two years ago,” Sand said during the debate.

“This is not about why you’re in Kansas. This is about the fact that you’re not in Iowa,” he added.

Lahn told The Des Moines Register in May that he regularly flies between Iowa and Kansas because he has a blended family, with children in both states. The Kansas Reflector reported that same month that Lahn, who co-founded a private school in Wichita, had previously voted in Kansas as recently as 2022.

Lahn has defended his residency track record in Iowa, saying he’s spends most of his time in the Hawkeye State and that he wants to present in his children’s lives. He told The Des Moines Register that if he were elected governor, there would be a “different arrangement” and that “we’d be in Iowa as much as humanly possible.”

“This issue is about one thing — it’s about my children. That’s it,” Lahn shot back during the debate. “I have a blended family, and they split time. And I’m going to tell you right now: I am not going to be intimidated on this.”

Lahn, meanwhile, attacked Sand over his wife’s familial wealth. Sand is married to Christine Lauridsen Sand, the chief executive of Lauridsen Group. The Lauridsen Group includes six different companies geared toward health and nutrition.

Sand’s in-laws, Nixon and Nancy Lauridsen, have donated millions of dollars to the Iowa Democrat , while his wife and other relatives have also donated money to his gubernatorial campaign. Lahn has self-loaned himself money on the campaign trail, though substantially less.

“Rob, you’re now encountering somebody who’s not going to be intimidated by how much money your family has — it just won’t happen,” Lahn said.

Lahn also brought up the culture wars during different parts of the debate, including accusing Sand of being in favor of promoting gender ideology and transgender issues in schools.

“You just in July were sitting with somebody who’s asking you if you’d be banning books on transgenderism in elementary school classrooms, and you said ‘no,’” Lahn said. “You said you’re not going to take on the culture war bills, which just means that you would allow a book on transgenderism to be put in an elementary school.”

Sand has said he doesn’t believe transgender girls and women should be playing in women’s sports leagues but has also objected to a 2025 law passed in the state that removed gender identity from the Iowa Civil Rights Code.

“You should not be fired from your job in the state of Iowa for being different. You should not be evicted from your apartment,” Sand told attendees at a town hall last year, according to The Gazette.

Sand gives shoutout to Nebraska’s GOP governor

The Iowa Democrat gave a shoutout to Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen (R) during the debate, lauding the GOP governor for investing heavily in the state’s public school system.

“Let me praise a Republican: The Nebraska Governor, Jim Pillen, actually put the biggest single investment in Nebraska history into Nebraska public schools. That’s part of the reason that they’re beating us now,” Sand said during the debate when discussing Iowa’s low-ranked school system.

Nebraska created the Education Future Fund in 2023 to offer additional financial resources to the state’s school systems that hadn’t been included in the funding formula for schools while easing property taxes, according to The Nebraska Examiner. The fund was created with an initial $1 billion investment, with the expectation that $250 million would be added each year.

However, the Examiner reported last year that because more funds are being taken out than being put aside, with a projection that the fund could run out of money by the 2027-2028 school year.

Lahn defends opposition to COVID-19 vaccine

Lahn stood behind his opposition of the COVID-19 vaccine during the debate, saying he talked “very specifically about the COVID vaccine and believing we need to pull the COVID vaccine off the market. I stand by it.”

The GOP businessman called Sand “COVID Karen” and said Sand was “lockstep with Anthony Fauci” over the issue, arguing the Iowa Democrat was in favor of mask mandates and locking down schools and churches.

Republicans have attacked Democrats over their past support for COVID-19 restrictions and mandates as officials took steps to curb the pandemic in 2020, arguing that those measures infringed on people’s rights and went too far.

Iowa Republicans have pointed to Sand’s previous posts supporting mask mandates and criticizing President Trump for pressuring governors reopen churche s during the pandemic.

“Setting aside the idea that the president of the United States has no authority to order governors to reopen churches, he’s tempting people,” Sand said in a video in May 2020. “He’s trying to make them feel pressure that they need to be in a building, that they need to be there. We don’t need to be in a building to worship God. We don’t need to be in a building to worship Jesus.”

Candidates find common ground on property taxes

Despite a contentious debate driven mostly by personal attacks, the two men appeared to find common ground on the issue of whether local governments should have more control over their property taxes in comparison to leaving it to the state legislature.

Both men signaled they preferred localities have more say on taxes.

“I’m a believer in local control in the vast majority of issues,” Sand said. “I think that the people who are closest to the people they are governing tend to do a better job because they know their communities, they know their strengths and weaknesses.”

“I think this is something that Rob and I actually probably agree on,” Lahn said later. “I think local control is a good thing. I’m glad to hear him say that.”

articles.title: Federal judge blocks Trump administration fines of up to $1.8M for migrants
articles.summary: A federal judge blocked the Trump administration's migrant fines of up to $1.8 million, ruling DHS unlawfully imposed civil penalties for ignoring final deportation orders.
articles.body: A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration's attempts to fine migrants up to $1.8 million for failing to leave the country after receiving final deportation orders. U.S. District Judge George O'Toole in Boston issued the ruling on Monday in response to a class-action lawsuit filed last year by two of the thousands of migrants who have received civil penalties from the Department of Homeland Security. The judge granted preliminary relief to the plaintiffs, finding that the administration's process for imposing the fines violated federal law, and that migrants in the "economically precarious position" of addressing the fines could be pushed into "insolvency." "The plaintiffs live in an economically precarious position even without the imposition of the government’s exorbitant fines," he wrote. DHS ISSUES $84B IN FINES TO ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION "They face the possible garnishment of their already modest wages, loss of any vehicles and homes, federal collections lawsuits and other adverse collateral consequences," O’Toole added. "If they were ultimately successful in this suit, there is no indication that simply requiring the government to vacate their fine notices would –– or even could, at that point –– make the plaintiffs whole or return the circumstances to the status quo." O’Toole, an appointee of former President Bill Clinton, described how the plaintiffs worked for low salaries and had come to the U.S. to escape political violence. "Nancy M. was fined over $1.8 million," O’Toole wrote, referring to one of the plaintiffs. "She is a laborer working over 60 hours a week with two jobs, and she reports feeling serious anxiety affecting her ability to sleep, eat and live a normal life." The judge also found that the administration's fine notices violated the Administrative Procedure Act by failing to provide specific allegations explaining why an individual's conduct warranted a penalty. Fox News Digital reached out to DHS for comment. As recently as July, DHS said it had issued more than 103,000 fines to migrants totaling about $84 billion since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. DHS has defended the penalties, saying people who refuse to leave the country after receiving a final order of removal could face fines of $998 per day. Although Congress authorized civil penalties under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, no administration had attempted to impose the fines until Trump's first term. Last year, the Trump administration began imposing fines of $998 per day for migrants who did not leave the country following a final order of deportation. The fines have been imposed retroactively for up to five years, with a maximum penalty of $1.8 million. 20 STATES SUE TO BLOCK TRUMP ADMIN RULE THAT WOULD MAKE IT HARDER FOR IMMIGRANTS TO OBTAIN VISAS, GREEN CARDS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In July 2025, DHS and the Department of Justice implemented changes aimed at streamlining the assessment of fines by scrapping a 30-day notice period and shortening the process for challenging penalties. The plaintiffs successfully challenged that policy and what they described as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement policy of issuing fines using boilerplate forms without independently assessing whether a person's failure to leave was "willful" or "voluntary." O’Toole also found that the administration had failed to comply with rulemaking processes in implementing its streamlined fine-imposition process because it did not offer the public a chance to first comment on the policy change. Congressional lawmakers have attempted to challenge the administration’s fines against migrants through the Immigration and Nationality Act. Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., and Dick Durbin, D-Ill., urged DHS and DOJ to pause the "improper application of certain civil penalties" in the law to "law-abiding immigrants." Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday said he would terminate outside consultants Chris LaCivita and James Blair if their work conflicted with the White House, following a report that the two were in the Balkans advising a pro-Russian political party and made hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Trump appeared to distance himself from the work LaCivita and Blair did for Republika Srpska, saying that it was fine for his consultants to have additional contracts but that he knew nothing about that work.

“Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants. They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. “They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them.”

“They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C.,” he continued. “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”

The New York Times reported Tuesday that the two went to Republika Srpska, a small self-governing territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The country’s elections are set to be on Sunday.

Blair and LaCivita were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars each through a Washington-based law firm that the Republika Srpska’s government hired to provide counsel on voting issues, the outlet reported.

While the Times noted that Blair and LaCivita were paid by the government and not the political party behind the government, it wrote that for all intent and purposes work for the governent and the party is the same thing.

The work was also notable in that it comes as Republicans are facing an uphill climb to save their House and Senate majorities. Trump has been traveling the U.S. to rally Republican support ahead of the midterms.

Blair served as White House deputy chief of staff but left for a temporary leave of absence in April to run Trump’s political operation for the midterms.

LaCivita previously served as a senior adviser to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.

articles.title: Here’s why to vote in midterms to give Democrats congressional majorities
articles.summary: Attorney A. Scott Bolden urged American voters to elect Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to counter President Trump’s policies and protect the constitutional system of government.
articles.body:
“Don’t count your chickens before they hatch” is an ancient proverb we should all keep in mind regarding the midterm elections. While pollsters and pundits say Democrats have a good chance of winning majority control of the House and Senate, this isn’t inevitable.

I agree that President Trump’s plummeting approval ratings , along with strong showings by many Democratic candidates in polls, indicate Democrats could flip control of one or both congressional chambers. But if many voters who favor Democrats skip voting because they believe their votes aren’t needed, Republicans could retain their congressional majorities.

In addition, if Trump achieves his goal of suppressing or invalidating many votes that would go to Democrats, Republicans could do better than expected in the midterms.

Trump — who still falsely claims he defeated Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election — will likely say Democratic midterm victories are rigged. He may try to overturn them, going to war not just against Democrats but against America’s democracy.

We must not let Trump destroy our system of free and fair elections. The only way we can stop him is to vote for Democrats between now and Election Day on Nov. 3.

Unlike football, which millions of us watch on TV and from the stands, democracy isn’t a spectator sport. We all have a responsibility to get on the field and cast ballots if we are to preserve our precious right of self-government and our other rights and freedoms.

GOP control of Congress for two more years would empower Trump to keep waging his senseless and costly war of choice against Iran, and continue his many other incompetent, destructive, corrupt and authoritarian actions. This would worsen the affordability crisis and all the other crises Trump has caused, and would endanger our rights and freedoms.

No matter what pollsters and pundits say, voting is necessary because election predictions are sometimes wrong. Don’t let them keep you from casting a ballot.

As the Pew Research Center reported shortly after the 2016 presidential election: “Relying largely on opinion polls, election forecasters put [Hillary] Clinton’s chance of winning at anywhere from 70% to as high as 99%, and pegged her as the heavy favorite to win a number of states … that in the end were taken by Trump.”

Trump’s efforts to suppress votes that he believes would go to Democrats — based on his baseless claims that widespread illegal voting is responsible for Democratic election victories — seek to turn back the clock on progress made in the expansion of voting rights.

Because of this progress , the right to vote that originally went only to white male landowners was gradually extended over many years to all white men, women and people of color.

In the civil rights struggles of the 1950s and 1960s, people of all races protesting the denial of voting rights and other rights to African Americans were jailed, beaten and sometimes even killed. Failing to vote shows disrespect and ingratitude for their hard work, courage and sacrifices.

Unfortunately, far too many Americans who now have the right to vote don’t exercise it, especially in midterm elections. As the nonpartisan group Fair Vote reports : “Voter turnout in the United States is much lower than in other countries, hovering around 60% in presidential elections and 40% in midterm election years.”

Voter turnout in 2018 was the highest for any midterm since 1914, reaching 49 percent. Turnout dropped slightly to 46 percent in the 2022 midterms.

Early and absentee voting is already underway in several states. In the time they have left, Democrats need to focus on turning out as many voters as possible who are sick and tired of spineless congressional Republicans who have ignored their duty to support our Constitution and the rule of law, and have instead given Trump a blank check to do almost everything he wants.

While the courts have acted to stop some of Trump’s worst abuses, Congress should stop acting like a rubber stamp for Trump’s every whim and do the job America’s founders gave it as a co-equal branch of government. Republicans won’t do this. Democrats will.

While he absurdly denounces Democrats as communists, Trump is trying to rule with an iron fist like the communist dictators of China, Russia and North Korea, whom he envies for their unfettered power and showers with fawning praise. This makes our president not just a national embarrassment, but a national security risk.

I urge my fellow Americans — including independents and Republicans disillusioned with Trump — to restore America’s true greatness by electing Democratic majorities in the House and Senate. There is no better way to protect our country from Trump’s misrule, and to preserve and honor our Constitution and the rule of law in the year we celebrate our nation’s 250th birthday.

A. Scott Bolden is an attorney, NewsNation contributor, former chair of the Washington, D.C. Democratic Party and a former New York state prosecutor.

articles.title: Ex-Trump personal attorney adds Dem operative as client, says DOJ treating him unfairly
articles.summary: An ex-personal attorney to President Trump is taking on a Democratic political operative as a client, accusing the Justice Department of not treating him fairly after he took a plea deal. Kendra Wharton will represent Colin Strother as he prepares for his Nov. 17 sentencing after pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering and agreeing…
articles.body:
An ex-personal attorney to President Trump is taking on a Democratic political operative as a client, accusing the Justice Department of not treating him fairly after he took a plea deal.

Kendra Wharton will represent Colin Strother as he prepares for his Nov. 17 sentencing after pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering and agreeing to cooperate against his ex-boss , Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas).

Trump pardoned Cuellar and his wife ahead of a trial on charges of accepting nearly $600,000 in bribes.

Strother wasn’t pardoned, so he is still staring down up to five years in prison. Now, he’s getting new help from Wharton, who argues the case should be dismissed.

“That resolution was beyond Colin’s control, and any frustration prosecutors may have with it should not be directed at a witness who cooperated fully from the outset,” Wharton said in a statement.

Wharton worked under Attorney General Todd Blanche on Trump’s personal legal team and later joined him at the Justice Department as an adviser. She left in July 2025 and now runs her own defense firm. The new case, which she called an “injustice,” puts her at odds with her former employer.

“Colin has suffered enough, financially and emotionally. He did what the government asked, and he is still being unfairly punished,” Wharton said in her statement. “His cooperation deserves meaningful consideration. We believe justice calls for dismissal of his case, and we intend to advocate forcefully for that result.”

The Hill has reached out to the Justice Department for comment

The Biden-era Justice Department indicted the Cuellars in 2024 over alleged bribes the congressman accepted from an oil company owned by the Azerbaijan government and a Mexican bank. The case was on track for a trial this year when Trump retook the presidency.

Trump pardoned Cuellar , holding him up as an example of what Trump says was unfair treatment by the Biden administration. Cuellar is running for reelection this November.

Strother is set to be sentenced two weeks later. His guilty plea — alongside one from a San Antonio businessman — marked a boost for prosecutors as they sought to bolster their bribery case against the Texas Democrat.

Strother admitted that in 2016, the businessman began sending him $11,000 monthly “consulting” payments he ultimately concluded were a “sham.” He acknowledged he was under instructions to transfer most of the funds, totaling more than $200,000, to the congressman’s wife.

Wharton said Strother had cooperated fully from day one and noted Cuellar’s pardon had bipartisan support.

“After President Trump said the Biden administration had weaponized the Justice Department against them, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries publicly defended the pardon, calling it the right outcome. The lead prosecutor on the case no longer works at the Department of Justice,” Wharton noted.

articles.title: Socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier excited for far-left power grab
articles.summary: A do-something Congress is about to be elected. They will not use their newfound power to curb government excesses so that no one abuses the office. They will go all out to enact their far-left agenda.
articles.body:
The GOP is cruising for a bruising in a few weeks, when Democrats have their shot to retake one or both chambers of Congress.

If that happens, rest assured that this will not be a Democratic-controlled legislature like any other in American history: It will be the most far-left majority the country has ever seen, filled with radical people who are committed to a destructive socialist ideology that sees the United States as a unique villain on the world scale, that prefers to root for communist nations like Cuba or even China, that sympathizes with Islamic extremists and believes America deserved 9/11, that wants to throw out the Constitution and borders and global capitalism. And they are positively thirsting for power.

Just listen to this recent interview with maybe the most radical figure of all: Darializa Avila Chevalier, a would-be House member from New York City. Avila Chevalier spelled out exactly what she will do when she gets into government: She will proudly and happily wield government power as she sees fit. In fact, she thinks that if Democrats have qualms about exercising power, they need to get over those real quick, so that her socialist revolution can become reality.

That was Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, another congressional hopeful, who was sitting next to her, articulating their theory that government power is a neutral force. I, for one, disagree, and disagree strongly. I think that’s putting the matter far too nicely.

The exercise of government power — government force — is an ugly, brutish thing. It’s some external forces taking your hard-earned money and telling you how to run your life: What you can do on your own property, what terms under which you can enter into contract with other people or other groups, how much freedom you really have.

Yes, unfortunately, is necessary to have some kind of government to defend us from external threats and to punish and detain criminals. That’s what our Founders envisioned for us: An extremely constrained federal government that was limited to just protecting our lives and our liberties.

Sadly, politicians in both parties have greatly expanded the purview of the federal government — and I certainly count President Trump in that camp. He has wielded executive privilege to launch new wars, impose tariffs and do other things that clearly exceed his congressional authority.

But listen to what radical socialists like Avila Chevalier are saying. They are not saying that Democrats should work to limit the powers of the government and keep reckless politicians in check. They are saying that once they have control, they are going to exactly what Trump does and then some: wield government as they see fit.

We know exactly what they are going to do. They will start by pursuing ruinous economic policies, like massive new regulations on the tech sector, confiscation of wealth from successful people, onerous labor restrictions and environmental restrictions that will make it even more difficult to buy a home or to start a business.

But Avila Chevalier plans to use government power for even more sinister ends: abolishing the people, the border, capitalism itself, and the Constitution — that’s what the charter of the organization she’s a member of, the Democratic Socialists of America, calls for. And she’s not backing down from that. She hasn’t renounced it, or said she disagrees with it. She hasn’t even said, well, it’s a nice idea, but we can’t do it. She wants to do it. And she is not going to be constrained by the idea that wielding power is an inherently unpleasant task — inherently contrary to our liberties. These socialists will wrongly say they are protecting your liberties, even as they enact policies that will make your life much worse.

How I miss the days when people running for office would at least make vague promises that they want to get into office so they can leave you alone. They often violated those promises, but at least they tried to express the sentiment. That’s all over now.

A do-something Congress is about to be elected. They will not use their newfound power to curb government excesses so that no one abuses the office. They will go all out to enact their far-left agenda.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Talarico steps off Texas Senate campaign trail after flu diagnosis
articles.summary: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico stepped off the campaign trail following a flu diagnosis as his GOP opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, launches new attack ads focusing on the Democrat’s absence. Talarico disclosed his illness at a U.S. Hispanic Business Council forum which he joined virtually, saying, “I was ready to eat my…
articles.body:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico stepped off the campaign trail following a flu diagnosis as his GOP opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, launches new attack ads focusing on the Democrat’s absence.

Talarico disclosed his illness at a U.S. Hispanic Business Council forum which he joined virtually, saying, “I was ready to eat my favorite quesadilla tacos, but I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago, and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas.”

He continued that he was diagnosed with the flu and was at his “most contagious” during the event on Sept. 30.

“I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail and so I want to keep everybody safe,” he said. “If I was passing on this illness to somebody and got someone’s grandmother or someone’s baby sick, I…couldn’t live with myself, so I thought the best thing to do was to put safety first and put everyone’s health first.”

In response, Paxton launched attack ads against the Democrat for his absence on the campaign trail.

Talarico’s last in-person public appearance was at a fundraising event on Sept. 28 with actor Robert de Niro in New York, according to one attack ad.

“Have you seen this man? His name is James Talarico,” a voice reads. “James Talarico has been missing for 11 days.”

Talarico’s campaign did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment on the attack ads.

Talarico is slated to appear at a CNN and Jubilee Media Town Hall on Oct. 14 in Texas.

Paxton, who won his primary race against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), is now trailing Talarico by 3 percentage points ahead of the November general election, according to Decision Desk HQ’s polling averages on Wednesday afternoon.

Texas is generally a red state though a tough midterm environment and Paxton’s previous controversies – including an unsuccessful 2023 impeachment on corruption charges – has created an opening for Talarico.

The Texas Attorney General is also facing backlash for leaked audios where he said the war in Iran and high prices at home are a drag on his midterm campaign.

“It’s not tariffs. … It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel,” Paxton told donors and lobbyists at a closed-door fundraiser, according to audio shared by Axios , when asked what issues were “dragging” on his campaign.
